chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
OppFi Inc. entered 2024 still carrying the bruises of the 2022–2023 non-prime consumer credit trough — a period of widened charge-offs and compressed margins across the sub-prime instalment sector. By the time chief executive Todd Schwartz presented full-year 2025 results in early 2026, two narratives had converged: a decisive credit-cycle recovery that produced record revenue, net income, and originations across consecutive fiscal years, and an unresolved litigation saga that had tested — and ultimately begun to reshape — the bank-partnership model at the heart of OppFi's commercial and legal identity.

## The Platform

OppFi Inc. ([NYSE: OPFI](https://investors.oppfi.com)) is incorporated in Delaware and headquartered in Chicago. Schwartz founded the business in 2012 as Opportunity Financial, building a technology, marketing, and servicing layer for FDIC-insured community banks to originate instalment loans to non-prime US consumers — those with FICO scores below roughly 650. In July 2021 the company closed a business combination with FG New America Acquisition Corp. and began trading on NYSE, adopting the up-C dual-class structure that has characterised it since: Class A public shares listed on the exchange, Class B shares held by founder-related entities, with operating-LLC units exchangeable into Class A on a one-for-one basis.

The principal product is OppLoans: instalment loans of $500 to $4,000, APRs typically in the 35–160% range, with nine-to-eighteen-month terms. Three Utah-chartered FDIC-insured banks — FinWise Bank, Capital Community Bank, and First Electronic Bank — originate the loans under programme agreements; OppFi purchases the receivables, provides the platform and underwriting technology, and earns servicing fees and net interest on the purchased book. The OppFi Card, a consumer credit card, extends the product suite; SalaryTap, a salary-advance product, was paused after failing to generate satisfactory unit economics.

## Credit-Cycle Recovery

The 2022–2023 charge-off spike drove OppFi to tighten underwriting materially, deploying an internal credit model it called "Model 6."

> "Our Model 6, developed from 2022 learnings, has better prepared us for economic volatility. We are growing at a comfortable pace with strong unit economics, targeting high-quality customers."
> — Todd Schwartz, Q4 2024 earnings call

The results bore the strategy out. [Fiscal 2024 total revenue reached $526 million](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/oppfi-inc-opfi-q4-2024-070917960.html), up 3.3% year on year, while GAAP net income more than doubled to $83.8 million (from $39.5 million in 2023) and adjusted net income rose 99.2% to $82.7 million — adjusted EPS of $0.95 against $0.49 the prior year. The annualised net charge-off rate for Q4 2024 stood at 54.5% of average receivables, 430 basis points below the same period a year earlier. [Fiscal 2025 extended the recovery into a record across every headline metric](https://investors.oppfi.com/news/news-details/2026/OppFi-Reports-Record-Annual-Revenue-Net-Income-and-Adjusted-Net-Income/default.aspx): total revenue of $597.1 million (up 13.5%), total net originations of $899.3 million (up 12.2%), net income of $146.2 million (up 74.4%), and adjusted EPS of $1.59. The net charge-off rate fell to 49%, from 51% in 2024.

| Metric | FY 2024 | FY 2025 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Total revenue | $526M | $597.1M | +13.5% |
| Total net originations | — | $899.3M | +12.2% YoY |
| GAAP net income | $83.8M | $146.2M | +74.4% |
| Adjusted net income | $82.7M | $139.8M | +69.1% |
| Adjusted EPS | $0.95 | $1.59 | +66.6% |
| Net charge-off rate | ~51% | 49% | −200bps |

> "Our record-breaking results in 2025 capped off an extraordinary year for the company, as OppFi achieved record total originations, revenue, net income, and adjusted net income."
> — Todd Schwartz, FY2025 earnings release

## The Litigation Crucible

Running through both recovery years was the company's sustained defence of its bank-partnership model against "true-lender" challenges asserting that OppFi — not its Utah bank counterparties — was the operative lender subject to state usury caps. The litigation map extended across multiple jurisdictions. Washington DC settled early: in December 2021 OppFi [agreed to pay more than $2 million](https://www.bankingdive.com/news/oppfi-to-pay-more-than-2m-to-settle-dc-interest-rate-cap-suit/610865/) — $1.5 million in restitution to more than 4,000 borrowers, $250,000 as a civil penalty, and roughly $640,000 in waived interest — and consented to cease originating loans above 24% APR in the District. California proved more protracted. The state's Department of Financial Protection and Innovation sought to enjoin OppFi's FinWise partnership as a usurious "rent-a-bank" arrangement. A California court denied an injunction in October 2023. Then, on 24 February 2026, the [Los Angeles County Superior Court issued a tentative decision granting OppFi summary judgment](https://www.pillsburylaw.com/en/news-and-insights/california-court-rejects-true-lender-claim-bank-fintech-partnership-dispute.html): the court found that FinWise had "retained control of core lending functions," held title to programme loans at origination, and maintained ongoing economic exposure — the substantive markers of true-lender status under prevailing precedent. The DFPI had 30 days to appeal. In the federal courts, the Ninth Circuit upheld OppFi's arbitration clause in May 2024, routing consumer class actions out of open litigation in multiple states.

## The Charter Pivot

The cumulative cost of that litigation — in legal fees, geographic attrition, management bandwidth, and persistent investor discount — supplied the strategic logic for the most consequential announcement within the snapshot period. On 29 April 2026, OppFi [disclosed a definitive agreement to acquire BNCCORP, Inc. and its subsidiary BNC National Bank for approximately $130 million in cash and stock](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/bnccorp-to-be-acquired-by-oppfi-in-transformative-customer-focused-transaction-302756718.html), targeting a Q4 2026 close subject to OCC and Federal Reserve approval.

> "The transformative combination of OppFi's digital-first platform and BNC's national bank charter unlocks significant opportunities for growth and product diversification."
> — Todd Schwartz, 29 April 2026

The deal would convert OppFi from a fintech service layer dependent on three community-bank partnerships into a bank-holding company operating under unified federal supervision — eliminating the jurisdictional vulnerability that had drawn state regulators into court for four years. BNC held approximately $1.1 billion in assets and $1 billion in deposits at year-end 2025; the combined entity would carry roughly $2 billion in assets. OppFi guided for adjusted EPS accretion exceeding 25% in 2027 and 40% in 2028, with synergies of $60 million in year one rising to $115 million by year three. A structural consequence would be the collapse of the up-C dual-class architecture — the signature post-SPAC governance arrangement that had given Schwartz and associated founder entities disproportionate voting control since the 2021 listing.

---

The chapters that follow examine: the remaining state-level true-lender exposure and the implications of a California appeal; OppLoans' unit economics as charge-offs track toward the 45–50% band; Schwartz's founder-CEO tenure and the governance transition that bank ownership entails; the competitive positioning of OppFi's product suite relative to Enova International, Curo Group, OneMain Financial, Elevate Credit, and World Acceptance; and the risk that acquiring a national bank charter simply relocates regulatory scrutiny from state courts to the OCC.

chapters.title: From 2012 founding through 2021 SPAC listing to the true-lender litigation crucible
chapters.body:
## The Chicago Bootstrap, 2012–2015

Todd Schwartz launched Opportunity Financial in Chicago in 2012 with a single animating premise: that the roughly one-in-three American adults who could not qualify for mainstream bank credit were not inherently bad credit risks but structurally underserved ones. The company's earliest incarnation was a direct lender, operating under state consumer-finance licences and deploying founder capital to make small-dollar installment loans to borrowers whom prime-focused institutions had systematically excluded by FICO cutoff.

The model was capital-intensive and jurisdictionally constrained from the outset. Licensing in each state required separate regulatory approval; rate caps in many jurisdictions compressed the economics of serving thin-file borrowers who carried statistically elevated loss rates. Schwartz recognised early that the path to national scale ran through a different structure — one that could harness the interest-rate preemption embedded in federal law for FDIC-insured depository institutions.

## Building the Bank-Partnership Architecture, 2015–2020

The pivot to what the industry calls the bank-partnership model — and critics have labelled rent-a-bank — took shape across the second half of the decade. Opportunity Financial entered into program agreements with a sequence of Utah-chartered, FDIC-insured community banks: FinWise Bank, Capital Community Bank, and First Electronic Bank. Under each arrangement, the bank originates the loan, standing as the nominal creditor and legally entitled to export its home-state interest rate to borrowers in all fifty states under the Federal Deposit Insurance Act. OppFi, operating as the technology, marketing, and loan-servicing layer, then purchases the bulk of each originated receivable from the bank, absorbing the credit risk and generating revenue through a combination of servicing fees and net interest income on the purchased portfolio.

The architecture had precedent — the model traces intellectual lineage to the export-rate partnerships that catalogue-era banks pioneered in the 1980s — but Opportunity Financial's execution was distinctively data-driven. The company built proprietary underwriting models incorporating alternative data signals beyond the FICO score: employment tenure, bank-account cash-flow history, and behavioural variables assembled to estimate repayment probability for the non-prime segment. Schwartz framed the AI-assisted scorecard as the core competitive moat, arguing that it separated the platform from payday lenders and pawnshops that charged triple-digit rates indiscriminately rather than tiering price to modelled risk.

By 2020, OppLoans — the branded installment product priced typically between 35% and 160% APR on terms of nine to eighteen months in amounts ranging from $500 to $4,000 — had achieved origination scale and a multi-state footprint that a direct-licence approach could not have reached in equivalent time. The three bank partners provided geographic breadth; OppFi's servicing and technology stack provided operational consistency that small community banks could not have built independently.

## The SPAC Window: FG New America and the July 2021 Listing

The company renamed itself OppFi as it prepared to enter public markets, shedding the Opportunity Financial brand for a tighter identity suited to a multi-product consumer-fintech narrative. The listing vehicle was FG New America Acquisition Corp., a blank-cheque company affiliated with Fundamental Global — the diversified financial holding company whose principals included Kyle Cerminara and Joe Moglia, the former chief executive of TD Ameritrade. OppFi's business combination with FG New America closed in July 2021, and Class A shares began trading on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker OPFI.

The transaction was structured as an up-C partnership flip, the dominant architecture for founder-led businesses accessing public markets via SPAC during the 2020–2021 window. OppFi Inc., the newly created Delaware holding company with publicly traded Class A shares, became the managing member of OppFi LLC, the operating entity. Schwartz and other pre-IPO equity holders retained their economic interest through OppFi LLC units paired with Class B shares in OppFi Inc. that preserved voting influence without proportional economic dilution. Those LLC units remained exchangeable into Class A shares over time, embedding the founder-aligned incentive structure common to partnership-flip organisations. A PIPE component provided additional capital at closing from institutional investors who underwrote OppFi's origination platform at a defined entry valuation, bridging any shortfall between the SPAC trust proceeds and the capital the combined company required.

The listing arrived at an auspicious moment in fintech sentiment but an awkward one in the consumer credit cycle. By mid-2021, post-stimulus household balance sheets masked deterioration that would surface in 2022 as fiscal support withdrew and inflation eroded the real incomes of OppFi's core non-prime borrowers. Schwartz rang the NYSE opening bell with a company that had achieved origination scale and operational infrastructure, but one that had not yet been tested by a full credit-tightening cycle in the glare of quarterly public reporting. CFO Pamela Johnson would steelman that resilience case across subsequent earnings calls as the cycle turned.

## The Litigation Crucible: True-Lender Challenges, 2022–2025

Within eighteen months of the NYSE listing, OppFi's bank-partnership model was under assault across multiple jurisdictions. The legal theory — known as the true-lender doctrine — holds that when a fintech platform prices, markets, underwrites, and purchases the loans while a bank merely signs the origination documents, the fintech is the true lender regardless of contractual form. If a state court or regulator accepts that argument, the bank's interest-rate preemption does not travel with the receivable, and state usury caps — which in California, New York, Colorado, and the District of Columbia can be as low as 24% to 36% — apply directly to OppFi's product, rendering the loans void or voidable.

California proved the most consequential front. The California Department of Financial Protection and Innovation issued an enforcement action challenging OppFi's partnership with FinWise Bank, asserting that OppFi was the true lender and that its loans to California borrowers violated the state's permissible-rate regime. The litigation forced OppFi to pause originations in California — one of the largest consumer markets in the country — and to defend the structural legitimacy of its model in court. Colorado, the District of Columbia, and other jurisdictions mounted parallel challenges, each with its own procedural posture and timeline.

The strategic stakes extended far beyond any single state. An adverse ruling in a major jurisdiction does not merely constrain originations in that geography; it generates persuasive authority for regulators elsewhere and emboldens plaintiffs' attorneys pursuing class actions on behalf of borrowers who paid above-cap interest. OppFi's annual reports catalogued the litigation exposure prominently, acknowledging that the concentration of bank partnerships in Utah-chartered institutions was precisely the structural feature that created preemption arguments — and the vulnerability to true-lender counter-arguments.

The company responded on three tracks simultaneously. It pursued appellate and trial-court defences of the bank-partnership model, arguing that decades of federal precedent — including the valid-when-made doctrine and the Madden-fix rules promulgated under the Trump-era OCC and FDIC — established that a loan originated by an FDIC-insured bank carries the bank's rate authority regardless of subsequent assignment to a non-bank servicer. It managed concentration risk across its three bank-partner relationships, ensuring that no single partner withdrawal would strand the origination engine. And it built a regulatory-affairs posture in Washington to engage policymakers on the treatment of bank-partnership platforms in an evolving federal preemption environment.

## Product Adjacencies: SalaryTap and the OppFi Card

Concurrent with the litigation challenge, OppFi attempted to broaden its product surface. SalaryTap, a payroll-deduction loan designed to reduce charge-off risk by attaching repayment directly to the borrower's employment income stream, launched as an extension of the platform's non-prime thesis. The product's logic was structurally sound — employer-linked repayment reduces involuntary default by intercepting income before discretionary spending — but the unit economics proved difficult to scale within the margins OppFi required. SalaryTap was ultimately paused, a footnote in the multi-product narrative rather than a second revenue pillar.

The OppFi Card, a Visa-branded consumer credit card targeting the same non-prime segment as OppLoans, launched as a more durable adjacency. Serviced through OppFi's existing underwriting and customer-relationship infrastructure, the card extended the company's engagement with borrowers who had graduated from installment lending or who preferred revolving credit. Schwartz framed the card as evidence that the platform could evolve beyond a single-product story — a bridge toward normalised credit access that differentiated OppFi from pure-play high-rate lenders with no graduation pathway for their customers.

## Into the Cycle Recovery, 2024–2025

By 2024 and into 2025, OppFi's financial trajectory tracked the broader normalisation of non-prime consumer credit. Charge-off rates on 2022–2023 origination cohorts, elevated by the inflation-shock period that had compressed real incomes and destabilised payment behaviour across the non-prime segment, began to age off the portfolio. The tighter underwriting standards introduced in 2022 — FICO floors raised, income-verification requirements tightened, approval rates deliberately reduced — produced better-performing vintages that rebuilt net revenue and returned adjusted profitability toward the levels the company had projected at its 2021 listing.

The recovery did not extinguish the structural question that had stalked the company since the first California enforcement action. Each adverse true-lender ruling narrowed the addressable market; each favourable outcome — whether judicial, legislative, or regulatory — expanded it. As of late May 2026, that balance remained OppFi's defining uncertainty: a Chicago-founded, NYSE-listed fintech whose operational record demonstrated it could build and manage a national non-prime lending platform, but whose legal future continued to hinge on courts and regulators resolving, state by state, who under federal preemption doctrine is actually making the loan.

chapters.title: OppLoans bank-partnership mechanics, OppFi Card, and the platform economics
chapters.body:
## The Program Agreement at the Center of Everything

Every OppLoans installment loan begins not at OppFi's Chicago headquarters but at one of three FDIC-insured community banks — FinWise Bank (a Utah industrial-loan company), Capital Community Bank, or First Electronic Bank. The distinction is not cosmetic. Under the program agreements OppFi maintains with each partner bank, the bank is the legal originator of record. It underwrites and funds the loan at inception, applying rates that reflect the home-state rate-exportation authority that federal banking law extends to federally chartered and FDIC-insured depository institutions. OppFi's role in that moment is service provider, not lender — it delivers the marketing channel that sourced the borrower, the proprietary credit model that assessed the risk, and the digital servicing infrastructure through which the loan will be administered for its full 9-to-18-month term. Within a defined window after origination, OppFi purchases the receivable from the bank partner at par. From that point forward, the economic exposure sits on OppFi's balance sheet, funded through the company's own warehouse credit facilities. The bank collects a fee for originating and holding the brief initial exposure. OppFi holds the interest-bearing receivable — and bears the credit loss if the borrower defaults.

This two-step structure is what OppFi calls the bank-partnership model, and it is the architectural load-bearing wall of the entire enterprise. It is also the feature that plaintiffs and state attorneys general have spent years attempting to demolish through true-lender litigation, arguing that because OppFi holds the predominant economic interest from the moment of origination, OppFi — not the bank — is the "true lender," and OppFi therefore should be subject to state usury caps that would render most of its loan book legally impermissible. The litigation thread runs through virtually every chapter of this dossier; for present purposes, the mechanics of how the model works under normal conditions matter most.

## Credit Decisioning in the Non-Prime Population

The borrowers OppFi targets — consumers with FICO scores below 650 who are largely shut out of prime credit markets — present an underwriting challenge that conventional bureau-based scorecards struggle to resolve with any precision. OppFi has spent more than a decade building proprietary machine-learning models trained on its own originations and repayment histories within this population. The models draw on an applicant's bureau data, but also incorporate alternative data signals: employment and income verification, bank-account cash-flow patterns obtained through permissioned data aggregators, and historical behavioral patterns from OppFi's own prior lending to returning borrowers.

The output is a tiered probability-of-default estimate that maps to loan pricing, maximum loan amount, and term. OppFi has maintained that its models identify meaningful creditworthiness gradations within the non-prime band that a simple FICO cutoff would miss — pointing to the existence of a "credit-invisible" or "thin-file" sub-population that maintains stable employment and consistent banking patterns despite a low or absent bureau score. This population, in OppFi's framing, is the legitimate addressable market: underserved by banks but meaningfully distinguishable from the deep subprime borrowers who will cycle through payday lenders and default at rates that make installment underwriting uneconomic. The empirical test of that claim is the charge-off rate across vintages; the 2022-2023 cohorts, originated during a period of looser credit-box expansion, produced charge-off rates that stressed the model's claims and forced a tightening of underwriting standards through 2023 and into 2024. [OPFI 10-K FY2023, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=OPFI&type=10-K)

## Originations, Servicing, and the Digital Stack

OppFi's consumer acquisition is predominantly digital. Borrowers arrive through affiliate marketing networks, search, and direct channels, completing applications through the OppLoans website or mobile experience. The decisioning pipeline — verification, underwriting, and disclosure — runs in near-real time, with funded loans typically disbursed within one business day via ACH. The digital-first model keeps the cost of customer acquisition comparatively low relative to branch-based competitors, though OppFi competes in a performance-marketing environment where cost-per-funded-loan can spike during periods of heightened competition from other non-prime lenders.

Post-origination servicing is similarly digital: payment collection runs through ACH debit against the borrower's bank account on a schedule aligned with pay cycles, and customer communication occurs via app, SMS, and email before human agent interaction. OppFi has emphasized a "no penalty for early repayment" and "no late fees" borrower proposition — differentiating from payday structures — although the APR headline (which can reach into the 160% range for shorter-duration loans) has remained the dominant narrative in regulatory and press coverage regardless. [OPFI 10-K FY2023, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=OPFI&type=10-K)

## OppFi Card and the Product Diversification Thesis

Alongside OppLoans, OppFi launched the OppFi Card, a consumer credit card designed to address a different need in the non-prime lifecycle — revolving credit access for everyday spending rather than the lump-sum emergency liquidity the installment product addresses. The card is issued through a bank partner and underwritten using OppFi's credit models. The strategic rationale was clear: the installment loan is episodic (a borrower takes one loan, repays it over 9-18 months, and may not return for years), while a revolving credit card generates persistent interchange revenue and recurring balance-carrying interest income, deepening the lifetime value of the customer relationship.

In execution, the card product faced the universal challenge of credit card economics for non-prime issuers: fraud exposure, credit-line management complexity, and the difficulty of building a card-spending habit in a population accustomed to debit. Through the 2024-2025 period, OppFi Card remained a secondary contributor to consolidated revenue, with the origination volume concentrated in OppLoans. Management has described the card as a product with a longer build trajectory than the core installment loan, and the company paused the SalaryTap paycheck-advance product — a third product pillar that had been under development — citing unit economics that did not yet justify continued investment. The contraction to a tighter product focus mirrored a broader post-2022 discipline around profitability over growth optionality.

## Revenue Architecture: Fee Income and Net Interest

OppFi's income statement reflects the two-layered structure of the bank-partnership model. The first layer is the platform and servicing fee that OppFi earns from the bank partner — a per-loan fee for the origination services, technology access, and ongoing servicing OppFi provides. The second, larger layer is net interest income: the spread between the yield OppFi earns on the receivables it purchases from bank partners and the cost of the warehouse debt it uses to fund those receivables, net of charge-offs.

| Revenue Component | Character | Primary Driver |
|---|---|---|
| Servicing / platform fees | Fee income, relatively stable | Origination volume; number of loans serviced |
| Net interest income on owned receivables | Spread income, credit-cycle-sensitive | Loan yield minus funding cost minus net charge-offs |
| OppFi Card interchange and interest | Growing; secondary contributor | Cardholder base and average daily balance |

The dominance of net interest income over fee income creates meaningful earnings leverage — and volatility — around the credit cycle. In a year of rising charge-offs, a widening loss rate compresses net interest margin faster than origination volumes can compensate. This is precisely the dynamic that pressured 2022-2023 results as post-pandemic credit normalization arrived earlier and more severely in the non-prime population than in prime cohorts. The 2024 recovery in profitability reflected a combination of tighter underwriting (smaller credit box, improved vintage performance) and the maturation of the problematic 2022-2023 cohorts through the loss curve. [OPFI 10-K FY2024, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=OPFI&type=10-K)

## The Up-C Structure and Founder Economics

OppFi Inc. — the NYSE-listed entity trading under the ticker OPFI — is a Delaware holding company that owns a managing membership interest in OppFi Units LLC, the operating entity that actually holds the receivables, employs the workforce, and contracts with the bank partners. This Up-C (umbrella-partnership C-corporation) architecture is the standard vehicle for founder-centric technology companies that go public while preserving the founder's economic interest in flow-through LLC units rather than converting immediately to a pure C-corp equity structure.

Under the structure, OppFi Inc. issues two classes of stock. Class A shares — the publicly traded units on NYSE — represent both economic and voting interests in proportion to OppFi Inc.'s membership percentage in the operating LLC. Class B shares, held by Todd Schwartz's founder-related entities and other pre-IPO holders, carry voting rights but limited direct economic rights in the holding company; the economic substance for Class B holders flows instead from their operating-LLC units. As founder holders elect to exchange operating-LLC units for Class A shares (a process OppFi discloses through 8-K filings with each exchange event), OppFi Inc.'s percentage ownership in the operating LLC increases and the Class A economic interest becomes correspondingly more complete.

The structure carries a recurring cash cost: the tax-receivable agreement (TRA) that OppFi Inc. entered into at the time of the July 2021 SPAC closing with FG New America Acquisition Corp. Under the TRA, OppFi Inc. agreed to pay pre-IPO LLC holders a substantial portion of the federal and state tax savings it realizes from the step-up in tax basis generated by LLC-unit exchanges. TRA payments are a real and predictable cash outflow that reduces the economic value accruing to Class A public shareholders from each exchange event — a feature that institutional analysts typically tax-affect when modeling free cash flow available to public equity. [OPFI DEF 14A, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=OPFI&type=DEF+14A); [OPFI 8-K filings, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=OPFI&type=8-K)

The up-C architecture also explains why OppFi's effective tax rate differs from a simple statutory-rate calculation: OppFi Inc. only recognizes the tax provision on its proportional share of operating-LLC income, and deferred tax assets related to the LLC unit exchanges reduce that effective rate further. For an analyst comparing OppFi's after-tax returns to those of a conventional C-corp lender like OneMain Financial, the structural differences in tax treatment require careful normalization.

chapters.title: Net originations, revenue, charge-off cycles, capital structure, dividend
chapters.body:
The financial biography of OppFi between 2022 and 2024 divides cleanly into two acts: a contraction phase in which the company deliberately sacrificed origination volume to protect the balance sheet from a deteriorating non-prime credit cycle, followed by a recovery in which the seasoning of tighter vintages, reserve releases, and disciplined expansion of lending capacity combined to produce the most durable earnings power the platform had demonstrated since its July 2021 NYSE listing.

## Net Originations: Trough and Recovery

Net loan originations peaked in the euphoric post-SPAC period of late 2021, when OppFi's bank-partner infrastructure was running at full capacity and pandemic-era income transfers had temporarily elevated repayment performance across the non-prime spectrum. By mid-2022, the picture reversed sharply. Inflation eroded the disposable income of OppFi's core borrowers—hourly workers and gig-economy participants typically earning between $30,000 and $65,000 annually—while the Federal Reserve's fastest tightening cycle in four decades compressed the spread between OppFi's cost of warehouse funding and the yields the platform could extract without breaching the implicit political ceiling on already-elevated APRs.

Management responded preemptively. Marketing spend was cut, underwriting score thresholds were raised, and OppFi's automated application funnel was deliberately throttled. The result was a sequential drawdown in net originations through fiscal 2022 and into the first half of 2023—a trough that the company characterised in its filings as a conscious "vintage discipline" strategy rather than a demand failure. [OppFi 2023 Annual Report / 10-K, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001818502)

By the second half of 2023, with the tighter 2022 cohorts beginning to season visibly better than the peak-2021 vintages, OppFi incrementally reopened the credit funnel. Originations ticked up in Q3 and Q4 2023, and fiscal 2024 produced a genuine recovery. Full-year 2024 net originations rose meaningfully year-over-year, with management noting on the Q4 2024 earnings call that the improvement reflected both deliberate funnel expansion and an underlying demand pool that remained structurally underserved by mainstream credit products.

## Revenue and Adjusted EBITDA

OppFi's revenue architecture has two principal components: interest and fee income earned on receivables purchased from its bank partners—FinWise Bank, Capital Community Bank, and First Electronic Bank—under the program agreements that are the legal cornerstone of its model, and platform or servicing fees earned for the technology, underwriting, and collections infrastructure OppFi provides to those banks. Because OppFi purchases the substantial majority of originated receivables, the loan portfolio sits on OppFi's consolidated balance sheet and interest income dominates the top line.

Total revenue—interest and fee income before provision for credit losses—held relatively stable through the 2022–2023 trough, because higher average yields on the tighter vintages partially offset the lower origination volume. The more volatile figure was net revenue (total revenue less provision for credit losses), which contracted materially in 2022 as the company front-loaded reserve builds against the deteriorating 2021 and early-2022 vintages. Net revenue troughed in the middle quarters of 2022 before beginning a multi-quarter recovery arc.

Adjusted EBITDA—OppFi's preferred non-GAAP profitability measure, which adds back stock-based compensation, depreciation, and certain transaction costs to GAAP operating income—followed a similar V-shape. The metric turned negative in the worst quarters of the charge-off cycle, recovered to roughly breakeven by late 2023, and posted meaningfully positive numbers through fiscal 2024. Todd Schwartz framed the arc on the Q2 2024 earnings call:

> "We've now demonstrated multiple consecutive quarters of improving adjusted EBITDA, driven by the intentional credit tightening we executed in 2022, which is now flowing through as significantly better credit performance across our portfolio."

The full-year 2024 adjusted EBITDA recovery reflected not only better credit performance but a fixed-cost base that had remained disciplined through the trough—the company had largely avoided the headcount expansions that complicated the recoveries of several fintech peers operating in adjacent verticals.

## Charge-Off Cycles and Reserve Dynamics

Charge-offs are the dominant driver of OppFi's economics and the variable that most directly links the macro consumer-credit environment to the company's equity value. OppFi reports net charge-off rates as a percentage of average receivables; the metric captures the fundamental challenge of lending at scale to FICO-sub-650 borrowers, where the difference between a 40% and a 58% charge-off rate on a portfolio of similar size and yield is the difference between meaningful profitability and operating losses.

The 2021 vintages—originated during peak-pandemic conditions when non-prime delinquency rates were artificially suppressed by stimulus transfers—performed poorly as that stimulus expired and inflation accelerated in 2022. Net charge-off rates climbed sharply through the year, breaching levels that had historically coincided with unprofitable unit economics at the cohort level. Management responded by building allowance for loan losses aggressively: the allowance-to-receivables coverage ratio expanded materially through 2022 and into early 2023, representing a balance-sheet acknowledgment that a portion of the existing portfolio would not be collected at carrying value.

| Period | Net Charge-Off Rate (approx.) | Reserve Coverage Trend |
|---|---|---|
| FY 2021 | ~40% of avg. receivables | Building from pandemic lows |
| FY 2022 | ~55–58% of avg. receivables | Reserve build — peak year |
| FY 2023 | ~48–52% (H2 improving) | Build pace slowing; partial release beginning |
| FY 2024 | ~38–43% (recovering) | Net reserve release contributing to earnings |

*Sources: OppFi 10-K and 10-Q filings, SEC EDGAR; approximate rates derived from disclosed provision expense and average-receivables data.*

By the second half of 2023, the tighter 2022 vintages began rolling off the delinquency curve faster than the provisioned loss estimates had assumed. This created the conditions for reserve releases—the accounting mirror image of reserve builds—in which previously accrued provisions are reversed into income as realised losses arrive below reserved levels. Reserve releases in late 2023 and through 2024 were a meaningful contributor to OppFi's reported net income and a primary reason the company's GAAP earnings turned solidly positive before the full benefit of the origination recovery was reflected in the top line. The 2024 vintages, originated under the tighter underwriting parameters codified in mid-2022, were tracking materially better on equivalent seasoning curves than either the 2021 or early-2022 cohorts—a data point Schwartz cited repeatedly as validation that the platform's machine-learning credit models were functioning as designed under adverse conditions.

## Funding Architecture

OppFi does not originate loans with its own bank charter; it purchases the receivables its bank partners create. Funding those purchases requires continuous access to capital, and the primary mechanism is revolving warehouse credit facilities—short-dated, asset-backed lending arrangements with major financial institutions that allow OppFi to finance its receivables portfolio at rates indexed to SOFR (replacing LIBOR post-transition) plus a lender-negotiated spread.

The warehouse book as of fiscal year-end 2024 consisted of multiple facilities across different counterparty banks, with total available committed capacity in the several-hundred-million-dollar range. OppFi's annual report disclosures described each facility as subject to borrowing-base limitations—covenants tying the drawable amount to the credit quality and performance metrics of the underlying receivables pool—which served simultaneously as a discipline mechanism and a potential constraint during periods of elevated charge-offs. During the 2022 trough, headroom under borrowing-base tests narrowed, which reinforced management's decision to constrain origination volume independent of any strategic preference: the funding architecture itself was signalling caution. [OppFi 10-K FY2024, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001818502)

OppFi evaluated term asset-backed securitisation as a complementary funding source that could extend liability tenor and reduce the blended cost of funds, but through the frozen snapshot date the company had not completed a public ABS transaction. Warehouse borrowings remained the dominant funding instrument, leaving the company exposed to facility renewal risk and spread volatility in a way that a term securitisation programme would have partially mitigated. Facility pricing became a secondary earnings headwind in 2022–2023 as SOFR moved from near-zero to above five percent; as the rate environment stabilised in 2024 and portfolio performance improved, incremental tightening of facility spreads provided a modest tailwind to net interest margin alongside the charge-off improvement.

## Up-C Cash Flows and Dividend Policy

OppFi's corporate structure adds a layer of complexity to cash-flow analysis that is easily obscured in headline earnings figures. As an Up-C (Umbrella Partnership C-Corporation), OppFi Inc.—the NYSE-listed entity—is a holding company owning an economic interest in OppFi Holdings LLC, the operating entity. Pre-IPO unitholders, principally entities affiliated with the Schwartz family and the management team that built the platform, retained non-public Class B LLC units exchangeable into Class A public shares on a one-for-one basis. Class A shareholders see GAAP earnings attributable to the public entity; the full cash generation of the operating platform is distributed pro-rata across all LLC units, including those held by Class B holders not captured in the public share count.

Two practical consequences follow. First, OppFi Inc.'s fully diluted share count—when all Class B units are treated as converted—is materially larger than its basic Class A count, a distinction that affects per-share earnings comparisons across periods as exchanges occur and the Class A proportion shifts. Second, tax distributions are made from the operating LLC to all unit holders, including Class B holders, to fund their share of the LLC's pass-through income tax liabilities. These distributions—flowing to founder-affiliated entities rather than to Class A public shareholders—are a recurring use of the operating entity's cash and are disclosed as related-party transactions in OppFi's proxy and annual report filings. [OppFi DEF 14A and 10-K, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001818502)

On the public-shareholder side, OppFi's board declared its first regular quarterly cash dividend in 2023, a deliberate signal that the platform had transitioned from the capital-consumption phase of the SPAC years into a cash-returning posture. The dividend was set at a level reflecting the board's assessment of sustainable free cash flow generation at cycle-appropriate origination volumes, with explicit acknowledgment in accompanying disclosures that the borrowing-base constraints and warehouse-facility covenants set a practical ceiling on how aggressively capital could be repatriated during periods of credit stress.

By fiscal year-end 2024, with reserve releases having bolstered retained earnings and origination recovery underway, OppFi maintained the quarterly dividend without interruption—a continuity management presented as evidence of the platform's durability through the credit cycle. The dividend was not large in absolute terms; the symbolic significance was disproportionate. That a non-prime installment lender, operating under a bank-partnership model subjected to litigation in multiple jurisdictions, could sustain a predictable shareholder distribution through one of the sharpest consumer-credit downturns in recent memory was, in Schwartz's telling, the clearest demonstration yet that OppFi had constructed something more durable than a cyclical origination vehicle.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
## The Complexity of Pricing a Litigation-Shadowed Platform

Valuing OppFi requires an unusual degree of structural clarity before any multiple is applied. The company's up-C corporate architecture — in which OppFi Inc. (NYSE: OPFI) is a holding company owning only a minority interest in OppFi LLC, the operating entity, while founder-affiliated entities hold the majority through exchangeable units — means that Class A public shares outstanding represent roughly a quarter of total economic interest. As of the frozen snapshot (2026-05-23), approximately 27 million Class A shares traded publicly against an estimated 105 million total fully-diluted LLC units (Class A plus Class B and other exchange-eligible units). Any valuation that anchors on public-float market capitalisation alone — approximately $250 million at a working price estimate of $9.25 per Class A share — systematically understates the implied enterprise valuation, which on a fully-diluted basis approaches $970 million. All multiples in this chapter are calculated on the fully-diluted economic enterprise.

The second structural fact is that OppFi's revenue is interest and fee income flowing through a bank-origination wrapper. Total revenue for fiscal 2025 is estimated in the $540–550 million range, drawing on trajectory disclosed in the FY2024 10-K and subsequent quarterly filings; management guided toward continued origination growth as charge-off rates on 2022–2023 vintage cohorts aged out of the portfolio. Adjusted net income at the LLC level is estimated at approximately $70–75 million for FY2025, with adjusted EBITDA in the $110–120 million band after adding back depreciation and stock-based compensation.

## The Multiple Stack

Against those estimates, OPFI's implied multiples as of the snapshot date are:

| Metric | OPFI (implied) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| EV / Revenue (FY2025E) | ~1.8x | Fully diluted units × price / estimated FY2025 revenue |
| EV / Adjusted EBITDA | ~8–9x | Midpoint of EBITDA range |
| P/E (fully diluted, FY2025E) | ~13x | Price per unit / estimated EPS at LLC level |
| Price / Tangible Book | ~2.4x | Against estimated book value ~$3.80/unit |

The price-to-earnings figure carries a caveat: because most net income is allocated to operating LLC unit holders rather than Class A shareholders for GAAP purposes, reported Class A EPS is artificially depressed. Investors analysing OPFI on a headline EPS basis will see an inflated P/E; the economically correct approach is the fully-diluted view above.

## Five Years of De-Rating — and Partial Recovery

OppFi went public in July 2021 at an implied enterprise value of roughly $800 million on the SPAC terms, with the stock touching $12–14 per Class A share in its early trading weeks. The euphoria was brief. Through 2022, a combination of deteriorating non-prime credit quality, rising cost of funds, and the first material true-lender adverse rulings in California and Colorado compressed the stock into the $2–4 range by early 2023 — an 80 percent drawdown from the SPAC-listing peak, and a multiple that implied near-distress assumptions: EV/EBITDA had collapsed below 3x against a forward EBITDA that itself was contracting.

The 2024–2025 credit-cycle recovery narrative produced a partial re-rating. Charge-off rates for the 2024 origination vintage improved meaningfully relative to 2022–2023 cohorts; reserve releases contributed to reported earnings. The stock recovered to the $6–10 range through 2025. By the frozen snapshot, the ~$9 working price implies OPFI has re-rated to roughly half its SPAC-era peak multiple — not a full recovery, but no longer pricing distress. The persistent litigation discount, reviewed in the true-lender chapter, accounts for the gap: the market has not re-rated OPFI to pre-litigation multiples, and likely will not until at least one major state-level legal cloud resolves definitively in the company's favour.

## Peer-Group Comparison

The relevant peer universe spans non-prime consumer lenders operating under various structural models:

| Company | Ticker | Model | EV / EBITDA (fwd) | P/E (fwd) | P / Book | Key distinguishing factor |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| OppFi | OPFI | Bank-partnership, installment | ~8–9x | ~13x | ~2.4x | Litigation overhang; up-C structure |
| Enova International | ENVA | Direct balance-sheet, US + international | ~7x | ~9x | ~2.0x | Larger, diversified product; no bank-charter risk |
| OneMain Financial | OMF | Direct balance-sheet, branch network | ~7–8x | ~9x | Leveraged; NM | Mature; significant dividend; branch-cost base |
| World Acceptance Corp. | WRLD | Direct balance-sheet, small-dollar | ~7x | ~8x | ~1.5x | Declining branch network; geographic concentration |
| Regional Management | RM | Direct balance-sheet, branch | ~6–7x | ~7–8x | ~1.2x | Smaller float; tighter credit box |
| LendingClub | LC | Bank charter, marketplace hybrid | ~10–11x | ~12x | ~1.8x | Bank charter provides structural advantage on state usury |

Several observations emerge from this table. First, OPFI trades at a modest premium to the peer group on EV/EBITDA — approximately one to two turns above Enova and OneMain — despite its smaller scale, more concentrated product mix, and higher regulatory uncertainty. The premium likely reflects growth-rate expectations: OppFi's addressable market, constrained but not eliminated by state-level litigation, still offers higher organic growth potential than OneMain's mature branch-network model. Second, LendingClub's higher multiple illustrates precisely what the market would assign OppFi if it achieved a bank charter or definitively resolved the true-lender question — a structural premium of roughly 2–3 turns of EBITDA for clarity on legal standing. That gap frames the upside optionality in OppFi's litigation trajectory. Third, the P/Book premium OppFi commands over WRLD and RM reflects the platform's technology economics: origination-cost efficiency and the absence of a branch network argue for higher returns on tangible equity when charge-offs normalise.

## Intrinsic Value: What the Current Price Implies

A simplified two-stage DCF, using fully-diluted units as the denominator, suggests that the $9–10 per unit price range embeds roughly 8–10 percent annual revenue growth through 2028, a long-run net income margin of 13–15 percent at the LLC level, and a terminal EBITDA multiple of 8–9x. That revenue growth assumption is achievable in the base case: if the core OppLoans product sustains modest penetration gains in states where the bank-partnership model is legally secure, and if the OppFi Card scales toward profitability on its own credit cohorts, the combined revenue trajectory is plausible. The margin assumption requires continued improvement in charge-off rates from the 2022–2023 peaks — consistent with management's commentary that the 2024 vintage was performing materially better — and disciplined operating expense control as the platform scales.

What the DCF does *not* embed, and what the market appears to treat as an out-of-the-money call option, is any meaningful benefit from geographic re-expansion into states currently blocked or legally contested. That optionality is real but unquantifiable; it does not need to be valued to justify the current price.

## Bull, Base, and Bear

**Bull ($14–16 per unit):** True-lender jurisprudence stabilises. A favourable appellate ruling — most plausibly from the Seventh Circuit on the bank-partnership model's validity — or a negotiated state-level regulatory compact in California and New York reopens two of the largest non-prime consumer markets. OppLoans originations accelerate to 15–18 percent annual growth; the OppFi Card scales to a meaningful contribution; adjusted EBITDA reaches $160–170 million by 2027. At 10x terminal EBITDA, fully-diluted enterprise value approaches $1.6–1.7 billion, or $15–16 per unit. The bull case does not require re-rating to SPAC-era multiples — only re-rating to parity with Enova.

**Base ($10–12 per unit):** The legal status quo holds: OppFi operates in its current state footprint, litigates defensively, and does not re-enter contested markets before 2028. Revenue grows at 7–9 percent annually driven by organic demand in existing geographies and gradual Card contribution. Adjusted EBITDA reaches $130–140 million by 2027. At 8–9x terminal EBITDA, enterprise value is $1.0–1.3 billion, or $10–12 per unit. This scenario is consistent with current pricing and embeds no litigation resolution benefit.

**Bear ($4–6 per unit):** Adverse true-lender rulings in two or more additional states — Washington state, Minnesota, or a federal CFPB action — materially compress the addressable market. Origination volumes decline 10–15 percent from peak; charge-off rates revert toward 2022–2023 levels as macro conditions deteriorate; OppFi Card is wound down due to capital constraints. EBITDA falls toward $55–65 million by 2027. At 7x depressed EBITDA, enterprise value falls to $400–450 million, or roughly $4 per unit — a level not far from the 2023 trough.

## The Consensus Gap

The market, as of the snapshot date, appears to be pricing a base-plus scenario: something modestly above the pure-status-quo base case, reflecting that the worst-case legal cascade has not materialised and that the credit cycle has clearly turned. What the market has *not* priced is the asymmetric upside from litigation resolution. OppFi's valuation today implies a roughly 70 percent probability that the true-lender legal architecture endures in its current form — neither catastrophically unwound nor fully validated — with the remaining 30 percent of probability mass split roughly evenly between resolution and escalation.

The dossier's read is that this probability distribution is too symmetric. The bank-partnership model has survived every judicial challenge to date at the appellate level; the FDIC's valid-when-made and bank-partner-primacy interpretive positions have not been reversed; and the OCC's Madden-fix rules, though challenged, remain operative. The more likely outcome is extended litigation stasis — the base case — rather than a structural unwinding. That positioning suggests the bear case is somewhat overweighted in the current price, and that a patient holder absorbs litigation noise at a price that would re-rate materially on any single favourable catalyst. The gap between that read and the consensus is not large enough to be an obvious mispricing, but it is directionally positive.

chapters.title: Quarterly cadence through the consumer-credit cycle and litigation milestones
chapters.body:
## The Reckoning Year: FY2022

OppFi entered 2022 carrying the shadow of its own ambition. The company had posted record originations of $758 million for the full year — a 27 per cent increase — and full-year revenue of $452.6 million, but the credit machinery that had generated those numbers was already showing fractures. Loans written in the second half of 2021, when competition for near-prime borrowers was intense and underwriting standards had drifted, began defaulting at elevated rates just as the macroeconomic backdrop deteriorated.

The pattern was quarter-by-quarter visible. In the first quarter, with charge-offs running at roughly 56 per cent of average receivables, net income slid to a loss of $0.3 million. Todd Schwartz, who had returned to the chief executive role, framed the miss as expected rather than existential.

> "While our first quarter profitability was muted as expected, due to elevated charge-off levels from loans originated late last year, our strong origination volume, improved credit performance and enhanced operating efficiencies provide us with confidence for the remainder of the year."

The second quarter offered partial relief: originations surged 57 per cent year-over-year to $226.2 million as higher-quality borrowers — pushed out of prime banks by their own tightening — migrated to OppFi's funnel. Net income reached $9.5 million. But by the third quarter the inflation surge was grinding into borrower cash flows, and a strategic reassessment was unavoidable. Management undertook what internal documents called the "July model adjustment," recalibrating the proprietary credit engine to screen out the highest-risk originations before they were ever funded. Early delinquency metrics began falling almost immediately.

The fourth quarter crystallised the year's tension. Revenue of $120.3 million was a record for any single quarter, but the net charge-off rate hit 59.3 per cent of revenue, and the company posted a net loss of $5.2 million. Full-year net income came in at $3.3 million — technically positive, technically the company's eighth consecutive profitable year, but a whisper of the gains that would follow.

Legal exposure compounded the credit headache. In March 2022, OppFi had filed pre-emptively in Los Angeles County Superior Court seeking a declaration that FinWise Bank, its Utah-chartered bank partner, was the true lender on California loans and therefore exempt from the state's 36 per cent rate cap under the Fair Access to Credit Act. The California Department of Financial Protection and Innovation (DFPI) responded in April with a cross-complaint alleging OppFi held the "predominant economic interest" and the arrangement was a "rent-a-bank ruse," seeking more than $100 million in penalties. Schwartz called the regulator's position "without merit" and invoked the 7.2 million Californians who, he argued, lacked access to traditional credit options.

## The Pivot Year: FY2023

The July 2022 model changes showed up exactly where Schwartz said they would. By the first quarter of 2023, first-payment-default rates for new customers were approaching pre-pandemic levels; by the second quarter, net income had reached $18.1 million on revenue of $122.5 million, a 90 per cent year-over-year improvement in bottom-line performance. The annual net charge-off rate fell from 51.6 per cent to 43.5 per cent of revenue — an 8.1 percentage-point improvement that transformed the income statement.

| Period | Total Revenue | Net Income | NCO % Revenue |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2022 | $452.6M | $3.3M | ~51.6% |
| FY2023 | $508.9M | $39.5M | 43.5% |
| FY2024 | $526.0M | $83.8M | 39.1% |
| FY2025 | $597.1M | $146.2M | 37.0% |

The recovery was not without cost. In May 2023, management announced the wind-down of both the OppFi Card and SalaryTap lines — the two diversification bets launched with fanfare around the 2021 SPAC listing. The credit card, originated through First Electronic Bank in partnership with Mastercard, had been classified as held-for-sale on the balance sheet since year-end 2022. The payroll-deduction SalaryTap product, which had expanded to more than 30 states through employer partnerships, was similarly discontinued. From the second quarter of 2023, all reported metrics reverted to OppLoans alone. The message was unmistakable: profitability over product breadth.

Schwartz was explicit at the full-year earnings call in what amounted to a manifesto for the cycle ahead:

> "We intend to pursue the same strategy and discipline in 2024. We expect to continue focusing on profitability over growth, and we plan to achieve this by maintaining prudent risk tolerances. We're not going to chase growth by paying more necessarily...you end up just getting a lot more high-risk customers."

On the litigation front, OppFi scored a significant procedural victory. On 30 October 2023, Los Angeles Superior Court Judge Dillon issued a 65-page order denying the DFPI's motion for a preliminary injunction. The court found that FinWise Bank used its own funds to originate loans, retained title throughout their life, and held a residual 5 per cent economic interest — insufficient under federal preemption doctrine to sustain the DFPI's "dummy lender" theory. The injunction denial did not resolve the underlying action, but it let California lending continue while the merits were litigated.

## The Acceleration: FY2024

With the 2022-vintage charge-off cohort substantially amortised and the tightened Model 5 and then Model 6 credit engines producing cleaner portfolios, 2024 became OppFi's first unambiguously high-quality profit year since the listing. Full-year net income reached $83.8 million, a 112 per cent increase, on revenue of $526 million. The annual net charge-off rate fell again, to 39.1 per cent of revenue. Adjusted earnings per share of $0.95 was nearly double the prior year.

The quarterly trajectory was steepening. In the third quarter, with net income of $32.1 million and a net charge-off rate of 34.3 per cent, the company posted the highest single-quarter profit in its history to that point. Originations of $218.8 million for the quarter approached the record set in Q2 2022. Average loan yield expanded to 131.4 per cent annualised as the portfolio mix shifted toward higher-quality borrowers paying above-average rates — a counterintuitive dynamic that reflected OppFi's risk-based pricing model selecting out lower-credit-quality applicants at lower acceptance rates rather than cutting rates.

In May 2024, the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit vacated a district court ruling that had denied OppFi's motion to compel arbitration in a California consumer class action. The Ninth Circuit's reversal, directing the district court to send the matter to individual arbitration, effectively extinguished the class-action mechanism for true-lender claims in the Ninth Circuit. Similar outcomes — arbitration compelled, class dismissed — had already been entered in federal courts in Texas and Virginia. The litigation exposure was not eliminated, but its practical reach was being systematically narrowed.

## The Record Year: FY2025

OppFi opened 2025 with a quarter that reframed the company's trajectory entirely. Revenue of $140.3 million and adjusted net income of $33.8 million — a 285 per cent year-over-year increase in the operating profit measure — prompted Schwartz to describe it as "record-breaking."

> "Our disciplined approach to growth, continued refinement in credit modeling, improved operational efficiency, and a strong balance sheet position us to deliver sustained, profitable growth in 2025."

The growth was not one-quarter noise. Each subsequent quarter expanded originations in the double digits year-over-year: $234 million in Q2, $246 million in Q3, $230 million in Q4. Full-year net originations reached $899.3 million, up 12 per cent, approaching but not yet breaching the symbolic $1 billion mark. Full-year revenue of $597.1 million exceeded the top end of initial guidance by roughly $3 million. Adjusted net income of $139.8 million was $44 million ahead of the initial $95 million guidance floor. Adjusted EPS of $1.59 represented a 67 per cent annual increase.

The charge-off rate continued its multi-year descent, reaching 37.0 per cent of revenue for the full year. During the third quarter, Schwartz was characteristically measured about the macroeconomic backdrop:

> "We constantly are surveying and looking at different data points...In our bank data, we're not seeing anything that would cause alarm."

And on credit discipline:

> "We have the levers to grow at double digits...We're very disciplined. We won't chase growth if credit isn't there."

The California litigation reached its own inflection point. In late February 2026 — within the frozen window — Los Angeles Superior Court Judge Gary Roberts issued a tentative ruling granting summary judgment in OppFi's favour. The court found that the DFPI had "failed to raise a triable issue of material fact as to whether FinWise Bank was 'merely a dummy' lender," dismissing claims under both the California Financing Law and the California Consumer Financial Protection Law. The ruling was subject to finalisation and a potential DFPI appeal, but it validated three and a half years of litigation strategy. What had begun as OppFi's most acute regulatory threat had, quarter by quarter, become its most visible vindication of the bank-partnership model.

chapters.title: Todd Schwartz, Pamela D. Johnson, executive team, and the board
chapters.body:
## The Founder Returns

The pawnshop encounter that Schwartz recounted most often had the simplicity of a founding myth. Sometime around 2012, Todd G. Schwartz — then in his late twenties, son of a Chicago entrepreneur, fresh from several years in California real estate — walked into a pawn shop and watched a woman in hospital scrubs surrender her wedding ring to meet a financial obligation. The detail lodged in his memory: the gap between the working poor and the banking system was not a policy abstraction but a lived transaction, conducted across a glass counter. "I discovered there are about 15 to 16% — roughly 45 to 60 million people — who fall below the 650 FICO score," Schwartz told the Tulane Freeman School audience in April 2024, describing what had become a set-piece in his public narrative. That observation was the seed of Opportunity Financial.

Schwartz, who had earned a finance degree from Tulane in 2004 and built roughly $40 million of multi-family real estate in California between 2007 and 2014 through his firm Beach Coast Properties, co-founded the company in 2012 alongside his father, Theodore "Ted" Schwartz, Managing Partner of Schwartz Capital Group, the family's Chicago-based investment vehicle. The elder Schwartz — a self-made entrepreneur whose firm had evolved from buying and selling radio time into a broader BPO and direct-equity operation — joined the board at founding and has remained a Class I director since. David Vennettilli, a Principal at Schwartz Capital Group who led the firm's private equity and real estate efforts, followed as a board advisor in 2015 and later took a director seat, completing what amounted to a family-office governance layer seated directly inside the public company.

Todd Schwartz served as CEO from 2012 until 2015, when he moved to Executive Chairman to make room for Jared Kaplan as chief executive. Kaplan ran the company through its highest-growth years as OppLoans, navigated the rebranding to OppFi as it built toward a multi-product platform, and ultimately closed the July 2021 business combination with FG New America Acquisition Corp. that brought the company to the NYSE. By December 2021, with the SPAC listing complete and originations at a record pace, Kaplan announced his departure: Neville Crawley, who had joined as president in July, was named his successor. Crawley [lasted two months](https://www.chicagobusiness.com/finance-banking/oppfi-ceo-crawley-leaves-after-two-months).

The [February 28, 2022 press release](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20220228005330/en/OppFi-Board-of-Directors-Appoints-Founder-and-Executive-Chairman-Todd-Schwartz-as-Chief-Executive-Officer) was terse. Crawley had been paid a year's base salary and his health insurance costs and was gone. Schwartz, then 40, combined the Executive Chairman and CEO titles for the first time, concentrating strategic and operational authority in the founder at precisely the moment the platform was entering a credit-quality deterioration cycle and an escalating state-level litigation war over its bank-partnership model. Kaplan retained a Class II board seat he held through the frozen snapshot period.

## CFO and the Operating Tier

Pamela D. Johnson became Chief Financial Officer in March 2022 — the same month Schwartz's new tenure began, and shortly after having already served as Chief Accounting Officer since June 2021. Her background was unusual for a fast-growth fintech: Johnson had spent more than a decade as CFO of Heights Finance, a six-state non-prime installment lender, from December 2010 through December 2020, and before that as CFO of Pioneer Financial Services, the parent of Pioneer Military Loans. She arrived with deep institutional knowledge of installment-loan economics and reserve-cycle volatility — the precise craft skills OppFi needed as net charge-offs widened through 2022 and 2023. By the Q4 2025 earnings call, she could point to a clean turnaround: "Model 6 has been a significant contributor to this growth," Johnson said of the sixth-generation underwriting engine. "Its enhanced predictive power has enabled us to better manage our loan economics."

The rest of the C-suite reflected Chicago's fintech ecosystem. Sal Hazday, who joined from ADP's Small Business Services division — which had managed payroll and HR services for more than 500,000 small-business clients — became Chief Operating Officer around 2017, bringing process discipline from large-scale, high-transaction-volume operations. Yuri Ter-Saakyants, with earlier CTO stints at Insureon and Beeline Solutions, served as Chief Technology Officer, overseeing the model and automation investment that produced LOLA, an AI-driven loan-origination-and-servicing engine, and the auto-approval rate that reached 79% by the fourth quarter of 2025. "We designed this to really make an impact and serve over millions of customers like we are doing today," Schwartz reflected in 2024, summarising a technology bet placed years before the results arrived.

## Board Architecture and the Dual-Class Frame

OppFi listed in 2021 with a three-tier governance architecture common to founder-led SPACs: an Up-C operating structure beneath the public holding company, a Tax Receivable Agreement (TRA) linking future tax savings to the Schwartz family's pre-IPO economic interest, and Class V voting stock that gave Todd Schwartz, through the TGS Revocable Trust and related limited partnerships, voting power disproportionate to his economic position in the Class A public shares. The effect was that the founder could not be removed by a simple economic vote from public shareholders. As of mid-2024, his beneficial ownership in Class A shares stood at approximately 32% of the class — material in itself, but reinforced by the Class V layer into effective control, per a [Schedule 13D/A filed with the SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1818502/000119312524183106/d870456dsc13da.htm).

The board's independent wing was designed to provide the credentialing and oversight depth that a dual-class structure invites scrutiny of. Jocelyn Moore, who served as Lead Independent Director, brought policy and community-development authority — she was Senior Advisor at the Local Initiatives Support Corporation New Markets Support Company in Chicago and Executive-in-Residence at The Gathering Spot in Atlanta. Greg Zeeman, CEO of Oasis Financial and a former Chief Operating Officer of both Enova International and HSBC North America Holdings (where he also served as Deputy CEO of HSBC Singapore), chaired the Audit Committee and brought specialist knowledge of specialty finance and consumer lending at scale. Christina Favilla, the third Audit Committee member, was a banking and financial services veteran with a track record in risk management, P&L oversight, and IT governance across volatile regulatory environments — precisely the profile suited to a platform living inside a years-long state-level true-lender litigation cycle.

| Director | Class | Status | Principal Affiliation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Todd G. Schwartz | III | Non-independent (founder/CEO) | OppFi |
| Theodore "Ted" Schwartz | I | Non-independent (co-founder) | Schwartz Capital Group |
| David Vennettilli | III | Non-independent (SCG Principal) | Schwartz Capital Group |
| Jared Kaplan | II | Non-independent (former CEO) | Board seat |
| Jocelyn Moore | I | Independent — Lead Director | LISC / The Gathering Spot |
| Christina Favilla | I | Independent | Financial services |
| Greg Zeeman | II | Independent — Audit Chair | Oasis Financial |

*Source: [OppFi DEF 14A FY2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001818502/000119312525103860/d920346ddef14a.htm), filed ahead of the June 2025 annual meeting.*

## The Governance Capstone

By early 2025 Schwartz's public register had settled into a consistent cadence: methodical, data-anchored, careful to reserve headline claims for underwriting metrics rather than macro bets. "We're building a leading mission-driven tech platform with a suite of best-in-class digital financial service products," he said on the Q4 2024 [earnings call](https://www.investing.com/news/transcripts/earnings-call-transcript-oppfi-q4-2024-beats-forecasts-stock-surges-93CH-3909402). "We're going to always focus on quality over quantity." When analysts pressed on the macro outlook, he declined to play forecaster: "We're not prognosticators of the stock market. We really feel strongly about our underwriting model and the development of it over the last couple of years." By Q4 2025 the results had validated the posture: full-year adjusted net income rose 69% year over year, and management guided 2026 revenue growth of 9%–13%.

The franchise he described — anchored in bank-partnership lending and proud of a net promoter score near 80, which Schwartz compared to Apple's NPS — reached its most consequential governance inflection point on April 28–29, 2026. OppFi announced a definitive agreement to acquire BNCCORP, Inc. and its subsidiary BNC National Bank in a cash-and-stock transaction valued at approximately $130 million, simultaneously collapsing the Up-C structure. The TRA, dated July 20, 2021, was terminated for a lump-sum discounted payment of approximately $40.8 million. All Class V voting stock was cancelled. Todd Schwartz's control — previously exercised through the dual-class machinery — was reconstituted as a conventional 32% economic and voting stake in a traditional C-Corporation headed, if the deal cleared OCC and Federal Reserve approvals, for bank-holding-company status. "The transformative combination of OppFi's digital-first platform and BNC's national bank charter unlocks significant opportunities for growth and product diversification," Schwartz [said at announcement](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/oppfi-announces-definitive-agreement-to-acquire-bnccorp-inc-and-bnc-national-bank-and-the-elimination-of-up-c-structure-302756614.html). "Combining our operations under unified regulatory supervision by the OCC and Federal Reserve simplifies and strengthens our compliance and risk management."

The arc was legible even before the deal closed. The founder who had watched the banking system fail a woman at a pawnshop counter had spent fourteen years building an alternative infrastructure — one that borrowed bank charters rather than owned them, and defended that arrangement in state courts across the country. The April 2026 announcement suggested he intended to close the distance between the two.

chapters.title: Non-prime consumer customer base, bank partners, and the marketing funnel
chapters.body:
## The Non-Prime American

OppFi's product thesis rests on a single demographic observation: approximately 48 million American adults are employed, banked, and capable of repaying installment debt, yet locked out of the mainstream credit system because their FICO scores fall below the conventional threshold of 650. These are not jobless or unbanked. The typical OppLoans applicant, as described in OppFi's annual disclosures, holds a W-2 position with at least thirty days of tenure at a current employer, maintains a checking account with active direct deposit, and earns a median gross income of roughly $50,000 a year. What excludes them from Chase or Discover is a credit file scored somewhere around 550 — thin histories, past medical collections, or the downstream wreckage of a single missed payment that lingers on a bureau for seven years.

OppFi does not run a hard FICO pull at application. Instead, it queries 500 or more alternative data attributes — bank cash-flow velocity, paycheck cadence, transaction merchant patterns, fraud signals, and device fingerprinting — to generate its own proprietary risk score. By 2024, the platform was automating 92.5 percent of underwriting decisions outright, rising to 93.7 percent in 2025, with the residual cases routed to human review. The credit bureau integration runs in the opposite direction: OppFi reports every loan to all three majors, positioning the product as a credit-building instrument as much as an emergency-liquidity one.

The loan product is deliberately simple. OppLoans are fixed-rate, simple-interest installment loans with no origination fees, no prepayment penalties, and no late fees. Principal ranges from $500 to $5,000; the average funded loan in 2024 came to roughly $1,900. Contractual terms cluster between nine and eighteen months, with an eleven-month average. What cannot be minimized is the cost: the effective annualized interest rate on OppFi's portfolio ran at approximately 156 to 158 percent across 2023 and 2024, representing the blended yield across states and vintages. In roughly a dozen states the company does not operate at all, precisely because local regulators treat that rate as usurious regardless of who holds the charter.

## Three Utah Banks and the Partnership Mechanics

OppFi does not itself hold a banking license. Every OppLoan is formally originated by one of three FDIC-insured, Utah-chartered community banks: FinWise Bank, which became the platform's founding partner in January 2018; First Electronic Bank, which joined in May 2020; and Capital Community Bank, which began originating in October 2020. Utah is chosen deliberately — the state imposes no substantive interest rate ceiling on consumer loans, and under Section 27 of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act, a state-chartered insured bank may export its home-state rate to borrowers in any other state, overriding the destination state's usury cap so long as the lending bank remains the "true lender."

The mechanics are tightly scripted. An applicant who clears OppFi's underwriting model is routed algorithmically to one of the three banks based on volume targets and a randomizing computer algorithm. The bank funds the loan from its own capital, holds it on its balance sheet for a window of roughly two to three days, and then sells participation rights covering approximately 95 percent of the economic interest to OppFi's special-purpose finance entities. The bank retains the residual — in California litigation, FinWise's retained slice was confirmed at five percent — and earns a guaranteed monthly program fee tied to originated principal. OppFi absorbs essentially all credit risk, books the receivables, and earns the spread between the portfolio yield and its funding cost across warehouse facilities with major bank lenders.

The program agreements are nonexclusive, generally carry sixty-month terms with automatic renewal provisions, and contain no minimum origination obligations on either side. By December 2024, the contract terms with FinWise, First Electronic, and Capital Community Bank were set to expire on February 1, 2026, November 1, 2025, and April 17, 2025, respectively, unless renewed. The absence of volume floors means any partner can throttle originations to zero without contractual breach — a structural exposure that OppFi's 10-K describes in stark terms: if a partner ceased operations or renegotiated unfavorably, the number of loans facilitated through the platform "could decrease and our revenue and revenue growth rates could be adversely affected," with a new-partner onboarding cycle running three to six months even under ideal conditions.

## Origination Concentration and the Shifting Mix

In the fiscal year ended December 31, 2024, one hundred percent of OppFi's net originations were generated through bank-partner loans, up from approximately 98 percent in 2023, completing the pivot away from any remaining direct-origination activity. The concentration among the three banks, however, shifted materially between those two years.

| Bank Partner | FY2023 net origination share | FY2024 net origination share |
|---|---|---|
| FinWise Bank | 34.2% | 31.8% |
| First Electronic Bank | 45.2% | 30.3% |
| Capital Community Bank | 18.3% | 37.9% |

*Source: [OppFi FY2024 10-K, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1818502/000181850225000003/opfi-20241231.htm)*

First Electronic Bank's share fell from the largest contributor to the smallest, while Capital Community Bank more than doubled its proportion. FinWise, the original and longest-standing partner, declined modestly. OppFi does not disclose the contractual or operational driver of the rebalancing, but the pattern reduces single-party dependency on any one institution — a partial offset to the structural concentration risk inherent in the three-bank model.

## Digital Funnel and the Lead-Generation Dependency
