OppFi acquires customers almost entirely through digital channels, with no branch network and a shrinking direct-mail footprint. The marketing mix in the year ended December 31, 2023 broke down as: strategic partners (performance-marketing affiliates, lead-generation networks) accounting for 74.2 percent of new loan originations; organic sources including search-engine traffic, email, and customer referrals generating 18.3 percent; and direct mail contributing 7.5 percent. By 2025 those proportions had shifted further toward affiliate dependency — strategic partners reaching 80.6 percent, organic slipping to 15.7 percent, and direct mail declining to 3.7 percent. Lead-generation affiliates are compensated at a negotiated fixed unit price per funded loan or as a fixed percentage of principal funded, creating a variable-cost acquisition model that scales with origination volume.

The trend toward affiliate concentration cuts in two directions. On the upside, performance-based affiliate channels allow OppFi to expand and contract marketing spend quickly, matching customer acquisition to credit-cycle appetite without carrying fixed-cost exposure. On the downside, increasing affiliate dependency raises the risk of partner disintermediation — a sufficiently large aggregator commanding enough routing volume can reprice its unit economics at renewal. Marketing cost per new funded loan ran at approximately $206 in 2022, falling roughly 20 percent through 2022 and continuing to improve through 2023 and 2024 as OppFi tuned attribution and shed lower-performing partners.

## The 40-State Map and the Contraction Zones

As of December 31, 2024, OppFi operated in 40 states — meaning roughly ten states plus the District of Columbia had been vacated or never entered. The jurisdictions beyond OppFi's reach cluster around two legal theories. The first is the Madden doctrine: the Second Circuit's 2015 ruling in *Madden v. Midland Funding* held that a non-bank purchaser of bank-originated loans cannot claim the originating bank's rate-exportation authority, binding federal courts in New York, Connecticut, and Vermont. OppFi offers no product in any of those states. The second is the DIDMCA opt-out: Congress's 1980 statute allows states to opt out of bank rate preemption for state-chartered institutions, and Colorado exercised that option through legislation effective July 1, 2024, capping rates on out-of-state state-chartered bank loans at approximately 21 percent. All three of OppFi's bank partners are state-chartered. Following the Tenth Circuit's November 2025 decision upholding Colorado's opt-out authority, Colorado effectively closed to the platform.

California represents the highest-stakes remaining battleground: OppFi disclosed that more than five percent of its finance receivables portfolio as of year-end 2024 related to California-originated loans. The state's Department of Financial Protection and Innovation filed a cross-complaint in April 2022 asserting that OppFi — not FinWise — was the true lender on California loans and therefore subject to the 36-percent-plus rate cap enacted under AB 539. In February 2026, a Los Angeles Superior Court issued a tentative summary judgment in OppFi's favor, finding that FinWise performed final underwriting from Utah, retained five percent of loan receivables, and exercised compliance approval rights over marketing — a factual constellation the court said the DFPI had failed to rebut. An appeal remained likely within the frozen window.

## Repeat Borrowers and the Refinancing Economy

The customer lifecycle at OppFi is defined by refinancing. The most specific public disclosure of the repeat-borrower dynamic emerged not from OppFi's own investor filings but from the Washington DC Attorney General's 2021 complaint, which drew on OppFi's own internal data to allege that 75 percent of the platform's pre-tax income from OppLoans borrowers derived from refinancing — borrowers who repaid one loan only to originate another, often within two to three months. OppFi did not contest the figure in the November 2021 consent judgment, which required $250,000 in payments to the District and approximately $2.05 million in combined restitution and interest forgiveness to Washington DC borrowers, after which FinWise ceased originating loans to DC residents entirely.

At the aggregate level, the arithmetic tells a similar story. Through the frozen window, OppFi had facilitated 4.7 million loans to approximately 1.6 million unique customers — an implied lifetime loan-per-customer ratio of roughly 2.9. That ratio both validates the platform's credit-building narrative, in that borrowers return because the product is useful, and sustains the economics of a business where first-loan charge-off rates can run above 50 percent of average receivables. The cohort that survives to a second and third loan carries a substantially lower loss curve than the first draw — the selection and seasoning dynamics that underpin OppFi's argument that it is improving, not exploiting, its borrowers' financial trajectories.

chapters.title: Where OppFi sits against Enova, Curo, OneMain, Elevate, and World Acceptance
chapters.body:
OppFi's competitive position was defined less by market share — the company captured a modest fraction of the estimated $300 billion US sub-prime and near-prime consumer credit market — and more by a structural wager: that digitally delivered installment credit, originated through FDIC-insured bank partners, was the durable architecture for non-prime lending at scale. Whether that bet held up against six materially different competitors shaped much of the company's story through 2025.

## Scale Is Not the Story

The first analytical mistake was comparing OppFi's balance sheet to OneMain Financial's. OneMain, spun out of the legacy Springleaf / American General Finance business and listed on NYSE as OMF, operated more than 1,400 branch locations across 44 states and held a managed receivables portfolio exceeding $20 billion as of year-end 2024. [Source: [OneMain Financial 10-K 2024, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=OMF&type=10-K)] Its typical customer carried a FICO score in the 580–680 band — meaningfully above OppFi's sub-650 floor — and borrowed $1,500 to $20,000 on terms that could extend to five years. OneMain was a direct lender: no bank partnership was required, no true-lender exposure existed, and its effective APRs — typically 18 to 36 percent — reflected both lower credit risk and the higher regulatory clarity that came with lending inside state usury caps. Its annual revenue exceeded $2 billion; OppFi's total interest and fee revenue was roughly one-quarter of that figure.

World Acceptance Corporation sat at a different coordinate on the map. The Greenville, South Carolina company operated approximately 1,200 branches concentrated in the Southeast and Midwest, with average loan balances in the $1,000–$2,000 range and a direct-lending model calibrated state-by-state to small-loan statutes. [Source: [World Acceptance 10-K, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=WRLD&type=10-K)] Its net loans receivable hovered around $1.3 billion. Like OneMain, World Acceptance was structurally insulated from true-lender challenges: its rates were set to comply with state law rather than rely on federal bank-partner preemption. The two businesses shared a demographic — the underbanked consumer with irregular income and limited credit history — but the delivery mechanism was inverse: World Acceptance required branch access; OppFi required none.

Both comparisons illustrated the same point. OppFi was not competing for the same customer as OneMain and only obliquely competing with World Acceptance. Its defensible niche was the fully digital non-prime borrower who needed funds transferred same-day, had already been declined by their bank, and would not tolerate a branch visit. The storefront incumbents, whatever their underwriting depth, could not profitably replicate that experience at OppFi's cost structure.

## The More Direct Fight

The instructive competitive comparisons were within the online installment and bank-partnership tier, where three names — Enova International, Curo Group, and Elevate Credit — came closest to matching OppFi's operating model.

| Company | Model | Typical APR (consumer) | Primary Channel | Managed Receivables (approx.) | True-Lender Exposure |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| OppFi (OPFI) | Bank-partnership (FinWise, CCB, FEB) | 35–160% | Online only | ~$750M | High |
| Enova (ENVA) | Mixed: bank-partnership + direct | 35–155% (NetCredit) | Online | ~$3.5B | Moderate |
| Elevate Credit | Bank-partnership (RISE, Elastic) | 36–299% | Online | n/a (private) | High |
| Curo Group | Storefront + online | Varies widely | Branch + online | Post-restructuring | Moderate |
| OneMain (OMF) | Direct state-licensed | 18–36% | Branch + online | ~$21B | None |
| World Acceptance (WRLD) | Direct state-licensed | 30–99%+ | Branch | ~$1.3B | None |

Enova International, OppFi's larger Chicago neighbor, ran the broadest platform in the comparison set. Its NetCredit brand offered installment loans to non-prime consumers at APRs overlapping closely with OppLoans; CashNetUSA served the shorter-duration payday and line-of-credit market; and the OnDeck acquisition of 2020 added a commercial lending vertical. Enova's total revenues approached $2.2 billion in 2023, dwarfing OppFi's comparable figure, and its combined managed portfolio spanned roughly $3.5 billion across consumer and small-business segments. [Source: [Enova International 10-K 2023, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=ENVA&type=10-K)] Enova used bank partnerships selectively for consumer products where state-law compliance required it, and direct-licensed models where it could, giving it greater geographic resilience than OppFi's more concentrated bank dependency.

What Enova's scale created, however, was also complexity. Managing simultaneous consumer and commercial credit exposure across multiple regulatory frameworks meant that true-lender litigation risk in the NetCredit business was diluted but not eliminated, while OnDeck carried its own volatility through the 2023–2024 small-business credit tightening. OppFi's narrower footprint — almost entirely consumer installment, almost entirely bank-partnered — made its risk profile less diversified but more legible.

Elevate Credit occupied the most structurally analogous position. Elevate's RISE installment product competed directly with OppLoans on price, tenor, and customer profile, while its Elastic revolving line of credit (originated in partnership with Republic Bank & Trust) demonstrated the bank-partnership model applied to a different product architecture. By 2023, Elevate had exited public markets, removing an explicit benchmark from the comparison set and signaling that standalone non-prime fintech platforms faced mounting pressure in the public equity markets at the prevailing interest-rate and credit-cost environment.

Curo Group Holdings provided the starkest cautionary data point. After completing the Heights Finance merger in 2022 — a deal that bolted retail installment branches onto Curo's existing storefront payday footprint — the company carried a debt load that proved fatal when consumer delinquencies spiked. Curo filed for Chapter 11 protection in June 2023 and emerged restructured, its ambitions of building a national omnichannel non-prime lender materially curtailed. The episode illustrated the leverage that storefront operators had historically used to finance rapid growth and the particular fragility that came with it when credit cycles turned.

## The Bank-Partnership Variable

Across the competitive set, the bank-partnership model was simultaneously OppFi's enabling technology and its principal legal liability. Enova used bank partnerships selectively; OneMain and World Acceptance avoided them entirely. The difference determined which regulatory map each company navigated.

For OppFi, the consequence was a constrained geographic footprint in states where true-lender challenges had succeeded or where regulators had explicitly limited bank-partnership lending. California's Department of Financial Protection and Innovation, Colorado's Attorney General, and analogous offices in New York and the District of Columbia each pursued actions that created lending deserts OppFi could not profitably enter. OneMain and World Acceptance faced no equivalent exclusion from those markets because their rates conformed to state usury caps. A non-prime California consumer who might have been an OppLoans applicant in 2019 was, by 2024, served either by a California-licensed direct lender at the 36 percent cap — if any were willing to underwrite her credit profile at that rate — or not at all.

Enova's greater diversification partially insulated it from analogous geographic constraints. Its exposure to any single state's regulatory action was diluted across a larger consumer and commercial portfolio. OppFi's dependence on bank-partnership preemption, concentrated in a narrower product set, meant that each ruling carried proportionately greater consequence for its effective total addressable market.

## Disruption from Below

The BNPL and earned-wage access adjacents — Affirm, Klarna, EarnIn, DailyPay, Branch — competed for none of OppFi's existing customers in the traditional sense and simultaneously competed for all of them. The distinction mattered.

A non-prime consumer who used an EarnIn advance to cover a $200 shortfall before payday had solved a liquidity problem without incurring the interest cost an OppLoan would have required. As earned-wage access platforms extended their reach through employer integrations at large retail and healthcare employers — DailyPay and Branch each signing institutional payroll relationships at scale — the addressable market for short-duration non-prime installment credit faced structural compression at its least-distressed end. OppFi's own SalaryTap experiment, which the company paused after encountering challenging unit economics, indicated that the company had tested this adjacency and found it more difficult to execute than anticipated.

BNPL presented a different dynamic. Affirm's and Klarna's prime-weighted merchant-financed model did not reach deeply enough into non-prime FICO bands to displace OppLoans volume directly. Their competitive relevance was indirect: by absorbing purchasing power among near-prime consumers who might otherwise have opened a revolving credit line and eventually migrated down the FICO distribution, BNPL occupied a buffer zone between the prime and non-prime markets that OppFi could not address.

## Where OppFi Stood

Against this landscape, OppFi's relative position in early 2026 was clearer in its constraints than its advantages. It was smaller than Enova by roughly a factor of four on revenue. It was less geographically secure than OneMain and World Acceptance. It was less diversified than either of those incumbents. And it operated a bank-partnership model that the broader legal environment had spent three years stress-testing in the courts and state legislatures.

Its claim to differentiation rested on the quality of its underwriting technology — OppFi cited internal data suggesting a meaningful proportion of approved borrowers had been previously declined by banks — and on the unit economics of a fully digital delivery model that carried none of the fixed-cost branch infrastructure that constrained World Acceptance's returns and that had, in Curo's case, helped produce a leveraged capital structure that could not survive a credit cycle. Whether those advantages compounded into durable competitive separation, or whether the true-lender litigation map ultimately confined OppFi to a diminished share of the national non-prime market, was the open question the company carried into its 2026 operating period.

chapters.title: True-lender doctrine, state usury caps, and the multi-state legal posture
chapters.body:
## The Doctrine and Its Teeth

For non-prime consumer lenders operating under the bank-partnership model, the true-lender doctrine is not an abstract academic theory — it is the pivot on which every state's addressable market turns. The doctrine's core logic is straightforward: if a fintech platform bears the predominant economic interest in a loan — marketing the product, underwriting the borrower, funding most of the receivables, and retaining nearly all the credit risk — courts and regulators may deem that platform the "true lender," regardless of which entity's name appears on the note. When that determination sticks, the platform loses the benefit of federal preemption that allows its FDIC-insured bank partners to export the interest rates of their home state to borrowers in states with lower usury ceilings.

The consequence is stark. A loan carrying a 160% APR may be entirely lawful if FinWise Bank, chartered in Utah, originates it and exports Utah's permissive rate environment under Section 27 of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act. The same loan, re-attributed to OppFi as the true lender, becomes criminally usurious in states like Illinois (36% cap), California (variable cap on consumer installment loans), or New York (25% civil usury ceiling). The litigation posture map of the United States was, in that sense, also the revenue opportunity map of OppFi.

## The Federal Backdrop: The OCC Rule, Madden, and What Congress Did

OppFi's preemption theory traced through a contested lineage of federal rulings and regulatory actions. The Second Circuit's 2015 decision in *Madden v. Midland Funding* destabilized one pillar of the bank-partnership model by holding that when a national bank sells a charged-off loan to a non-bank, the non-bank cannot rely on the originating bank's federal preemption to enforce the original interest rate. Though *Madden* was formally limited to the Second Circuit and addressed loan transfers rather than origination partnerships, it seeded the legal vocabulary that state attorneys general and regulators would later deploy against fintechs.

In October 2020, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency issued a [True Lender final rule](https://www.occ.gov/news-issuances/news-releases/2020/nr-occ-2020-140.html) providing a safe harbor for national banks: a national bank is the true lender if it is named as lender in the loan agreement or funds the loan at origination. Consumer advocates and a coalition of state attorneys general opposed the rule vigorously. In May 2021, the Senate voted to overturn it under the Congressional Review Act, and President Biden signed the repeal into law. The repeal applied only to the OCC's rule for nationally chartered banks; it did not formally affect FDIC-insured state-chartered banks — OppFi's actual partners — whose legal footing rested on Section 27 of the FDIA and the FDIC's companion "Valid When Made" regulation. But the political signal was unmistakable: Congress had declared that the federal government would not supply the rent-a-bank safe harbor. State regulators heard the message clearly.

## Illinois: The Home-State Wound

No state-level development cut more sharply than Illinois. In March 2021, Governor J.B. Pritzker signed the [Predatory Loan Prevention Act](https://www.ilga.gov/legislation/publicacts/101/PDF/101-0658.pdf) into law. The PLPA imposed a 36% APR cap — modeled on the federal Military Lending Act ceiling — on virtually all consumer loans, explicitly including loans made through bank partnerships. The statute's drafters had anticipated the rent-a-bank workaround and foreclosed it by name: the rate cap applied to any entity that was "the lender with respect to a consumer loan," whether or not that entity was an FDIC-insured depository institution.

OppFi challenged the PLPA in the Northern District of Illinois, arguing that Section 27 of the FDIA preempted the state cap as applied to loans originated by its FDIC-insured bank partners. Federal courts declined to sustain the preemption argument as applied to the bank-partnership structure OppFi operated under. OppFi suspended new lending to Illinois residents — a not-inconsequential blow for a company headquartered in Chicago — and disclosed the withdrawal in its subsequent annual filings with the [SEC](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001818502&type=10-K&dateb=&owner=include&count=40). Illinois remained a closed market through the frozen snapshot date, with no legislative resolution restoring OppFi's ability to originate in its home state.

## California: The DFPI's Offensive

California represented the largest prize and the sharpest regulatory sword. The California Department of Financial Protection and Innovation, fortified by expanded authority under the [California Consumer Financial Protection Law](https://dfpi.ca.gov/california-consumer-financial-protection-law/) enacted in 2020, trained its examination and enforcement apparatus on fintech lending partnerships beginning in earnest in 2022 and 2023.

The DFPI's theory tracked the true-lender doctrine directly: OppFi, not its Utah bank partners, bore the material economic interest in the loans — designing the credit model, marketing to borrowers, funding the receivables purchased from the bank partners under program agreements, and retaining the credit risk on its balance sheet. Under that analysis, OppFi required a California Financing Law license and its loans were subject to California's consumer lending rate restrictions. OppFi disputed the characterization, contending that its bank partners were the originating lenders entitled to export their home-state rates under federal law and that California's application of state usury principles was preempted.

The dispute evolved into administrative proceedings and parallel litigation. OppFi disclosed the California proceedings in its SEC filings as a material contingency, flagging the potential for an adverse determination to require suspension of new originations in the state. California accounted for a meaningful share of OppFi's total loan volume; the loss of access would have ranked among the largest single-state contractions in its operating history. By mid-2025, the California proceedings remained at the contested stage, with OppFi maintaining lending operations under the bank-partnership structure while litigation advanced. The DFPI had not obtained a final injunction or entered a final order as of the frozen snapshot date, though the administrative calendar was moving forward.

## Colorado: The Statutory True-Lender Path

Colorado took a different approach, codifying the true-lender standard in statute rather than relying on regulators to extrapolate it from existing law. [Senate Bill 21-093](https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/sb21-093), signed into law in 2021, created a statutory true-lender test under Colorado law: if a non-bank entity has the predominant economic interest in a loan — a defined standard incorporating risk retention, marketing, underwriting, and funding — that entity is the lender for purposes of Colorado's Uniform Consumer Credit Code rate restrictions.

Colorado's statutory codification was significant because it foreclosed the preemption argument at the definitional level. Unlike California, where OppFi could contest the DFPI's regulatory interpretation of existing law, Colorado's legislature had directly addressed and rejected the bank-export structure as applied to partnerships in which the fintech bore the predominant economic interest. The Colorado Attorney General pursued enforcement against rent-a-bank lenders following the bill's enactment, and OppFi disclosed Colorado among the jurisdictions where its ability to originate new loans faced ongoing legal challenge.

## Washington D.C. and the Eastern Seaboard Pressure

The District of Columbia enacted the True Lender Amendment Act, aligning D.C. lending law with the true-lender framework and enabling the D.C. Attorney General to pursue enforcement actions against fintech lenders operating under bank partnerships. OppFi disclosed D.C. proceedings in its public filings as part of its expanding multi-state litigation inventory.

New York presented structural rather than active enforcement pressure. New York's 25% civil usury cap for most consumer loans and its criminal usury provisions had long made the state effectively inaccessible to high-APR consumer lenders operating through any structure. The New York Department of Financial Services and the Office of the Attorney General had pursued enforcement against various rent-a-bank arrangements, and New York remained outside OppFi's addressable footprint throughout the 2021–2025 period. Minnesota and North Carolina emerged as active enforcement states by 2024, narrowing OppFi's accessible geography further.

## Addressable Market Compression

The cumulative effect of multi-state true-lender challenges was a progressive contraction in OppFi's available market. In its 2022, 2023, and 2024 annual filings, OppFi disclosed that it was not operating, had suspended operations, or faced material legal uncertainty in an expanding list of states, enumerating the jurisdictions as risk factors and flagging that adverse judicial or regulatory outcomes could require suspension of new originations pending appeal or statutory change.

| Jurisdiction | Status (as of frozen snapshot) | Legal Vehicle |
|---|---|---|
| Illinois | Suspended; litigation exhausted | PLPA statutory 36% cap; preemption challenge declined |
| California | Active but contested | CCFPL / DFPI administrative proceedings |
| Colorado | Restricted | SB 21-093 statutory true-lender test |
| Washington, D.C. | Restricted | True Lender Amendment Act; AG enforcement |
| New York | Not operating | Criminal usury; DFS/AG posture |
| Minnesota | Restricted | AG consumer-protection enforcement |
| North Carolina | Restricted | AG proceedings |

Each line in that table represented a population cohort of non-prime consumers that OppFi's underwriting algorithm could serve but its legal posture precluded. For a company whose total addressable market is defined by geography and APR tolerance, each adverse determination was simultaneously a legal loss and a revenue ceiling.

## Federal Crosscurrents: The CFPB's Arc

At the federal level, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau under Director Rohit Chopra was a consistent adversary of the bank-partnership model through 2024. The Bureau filed amicus briefs in state and federal litigation supporting true-lender arguments, used its supervisory authority to examine bank partners involved in fintech arrangements, and issued guidance signaling its view that non-bank platforms bearing predominant economic interest were the de facto lenders for consumer-protection purposes. OppFi's bank partners — FinWise, Capital Community, and First Electronic — all fell within the Bureau's examination reach as insured depositories, and the CFPB's scrutiny of program agreements added a federal dimension to what had primarily been a state-level fight.

The inauguration of the Trump administration in January 2025 altered the federal vector sharply. Chopra was dismissed, and the CFPB's leadership and posture shifted under acting directors aligned with the new administration's deregulatory philosophy. The Bureau's amicus practice in rent-a-bank cases softened materially, and active examination of bank-partnership structures decelerated. By mid-2025, CFPB enforcement activity against OppFi's category of lender had substantially diminished — though the structural hostility built into state statutes like Illinois's PLPA and Colorado's SB 21-093 remained unchanged regardless of federal posture. State law, once enacted, did not pivot with the federal political cycle.

## OppFi's Strategic Response and the Residual Wager

Against this backdrop, OppFi pursued a three-track legal strategy. The first track was litigation: challenging adverse state determinations in federal and state court, arguing Section 27 FDIA preemption and, where possible, procedural infirmities in the regulatory process. The second track was engagement: working with state legislators and regulators to negotiate operating parameters — rate schedules, disclosure requirements, or licensing arrangements — that could allow continued lending within a compliant framework. The third track was market prioritization: concentrating origination volume in lower-legal-risk jurisdictions, accepting compressed geography in exchange for operational clarity.

Schwartz addressed the litigation environment repeatedly on earnings calls, characterizing OppFi's bank partners as the genuine originating lenders under a documented and substantive program structure, disputing the regulatory characterizations of the partnership as a mere conduit. The company's legal disclosures throughout the 2022–2025 period consistently maintained that the bank-partnership model was lawful under applicable federal preemption doctrine while acknowledging the material risk that adverse outcomes could reduce operating markets and revenue.

The structural bet — that the bank-partnership model would survive state-level challenge in enough jurisdictions to sustain a viable national footprint — remained the central, unresolved wager of the OppFi investment thesis through the frozen snapshot. Each court docket and each state legislative session carried the potential to expand or contract the company's effective market by millions of eligible borrowers and tens of millions of dollars in potential originations. The litigation map was, inescapably, the business map.

chapters.title: Timeline from 2012 founding through SPAC listing and litigation milestones
chapters.body:
## From Kitchen Table to Capital Markets: The Founding Proposition

Todd Schwartz launched Opportunity Financial out of Chicago in 2012 with a thesis that mainstream consumer lending had abandoned a substantial and creditworthy segment of the American workforce. The target was non-prime borrowers — consumers with FICO scores below 650 who were not reckless, but rather salaried, employed Americans who sat just outside the scoring thresholds at which large banks competed for business. Their alternatives were payday lenders: short-term, high-fee, structurally punishing products that extracted rather than served. Schwartz's proposition was a longer-tenor installment loan — later standardized as OppLoans, typically $500 to $4,000 at terms of nine to eighteen months — that could report to credit bureaus, build borrower credit histories, and carry APRs calibrated to actual underwriting risk rather than the triple-digit floor of the payday world.

The business model built around that proposition was architecturally distinctive from the outset. OppFi would not hold lending licenses directly in most states. Instead, it would partner with FDIC-insured community banks — FinWise Bank, later Capital Community Bank and First Electronic Bank — and function as the technology, marketing, and servicing layer. The partner banks made the nominal credit decision and originated the loans; OppFi then purchased a substantial portion of those receivables under program agreements and earned platform and servicing fees on the remainder. That structure was not accidental. Federal banking law — specifically the National Bank Act and the Federal Deposit Insurance Act, as interpreted through the so-called valid-when-made doctrine — allowed loans originated by federally regulated banks to carry interest rates that might exceed individual state usury caps, because the bank's charter, not the state, defined permissible rates. OppFi built an entire platform around that legal architecture.

## The SPAC Pivot and the NYSE Listing

For nearly a decade, Opportunity Financial operated privately, scaling originations and refining its credit model across economic cycles. By 2020, with blank-check SPAC vehicles flooding capital markets in search of fintech merger targets, Schwartz and his investors made the decision to take the company public through a combination with FG New America Acquisition Corp., a SPAC sponsored by FG Group Holdings. The transaction closed in July 2021, and OppFi's Class A shares began trading on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker OPFI.

The corporate structure that emerged was an up-C arrangement — standard for founder-led fintech SPACs of that vintage — in which OppFi Inc. served as a publicly traded holding company owning an interest in the operating LLC. Schwartz and founder-affiliated entities retained Class B shares and operating-LLC units exchangeable into Class A shares, preserving economic and voting leverage while the public float circulated Class A stock. The arrangement carried immediate consequences for cash management: tax distributions to operating-LLC unit holders became a recurring use of cash alongside the dividend OppFi subsequently declared to Class A shareholders.

The timing of the listing proved, in retrospect, almost precisely wrong. The July 2021 close arrived as the Federal Reserve was still months away from its first post-pandemic rate increase, and credit markets were pricing non-prime consumer risk with the optimism characteristic of a late-cycle run. OppFi entered the public markets with fresh capital and an expansionist agenda at the moment the credit cycle was about to inflect adversely.

## True-Lender Litigation: The Long Reckoning

Even before the listing, state attorneys general and consumer-finance regulators had been assembling challenges to the bank-partnership model on which OppFi and its peers depended. The argument was that OppFi — not its bank partners — was the "true lender" on the loans it serviced and largely funded, because it bore the predominant economic interest in the receivables, designed the product, and conducted the marketing. If OppFi were the true lender, it would be subject to state usury caps and licensing requirements regardless of the bank partner's nominal origination role.

The challenges were not abstract. California's Department of Financial Protection and Innovation pressed the true-lender theory against multiple fintech lenders. Colorado enacted legislation explicitly targeting the bank-partnership model and requiring non-bank partners to obtain state licenses. New York regulators and the District of Columbia pursued parallel lines of inquiry. OppFi disclosed its ongoing state-level exposure across successive 10-K filings with the [SEC](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=OPFI&type=10-K), cataloguing jurisdictions in which its bank-partnership model faced challenge.

Each adverse state-level outcome compressed the addressable market directly: a true-lender finding in a major state meant either winding down originations there, accepting state-capped rates that made the non-prime segment economically unviable, or litigating through appeals. The risk profile was not symmetric in the other direction. A favorable ruling preserved originations and potentially established useful precedent; an adverse ruling created pressure for pricing changes, geographic retreat, or structural modification — all carrying revenue and cost consequences visible in the following quarters' financial statements.

## The Credit-Cycle Trough: 2022–2023

Simultaneous with the true-lender litigation, OppFi navigated the most difficult credit environment for non-prime consumer lending in more than a decade. The 2022 and 2023 loan vintages experienced elevated charge-off rates as pandemic-era excess savings depleted, real wages lagged shelter and food inflation, and borrowers across the credit spectrum showed rising delinquency. OppFi built provision expense aggressively through that period, alongside peers including Enova International, Curo Group, OneMain Financial, and Elevate Credit.

Product expansion ambitions were simultaneously recalibrated. SalaryTap, the salary-advance product OppFi had introduced as a complement to OppLoans, was paused following challenging unit economics — the first visible evidence that the multi-product ambition carried meaningful execution risk. The OppFi Card, a consumer revolving-credit product, remained active as the company's principal second product, designed to serve borrowers who had graduated from installment credit and sought a longer-tenor credit relationship.

## The 2024 Recovery and the Restored Unit Economics

By fiscal 2024, the mature vintage cohorts from the 2022–2023 stress period were rolling through the loss-recognition window, and new originations were underwritten to tighter criteria reflecting the lessons of those vintages. Revenue scaled relative to the trough year, charge-off rates moderated as portfolio mix shifted toward better-performing 2024 cohorts, and profitability turned sustainably positive after two years of compressed margins. The directional improvement was sufficient to restore investor confidence in the platform's unit economics, even as the broader non-prime consumer remained under household budget pressure.

## Forward Catalysts and the Contested Horizon

As of the frozen snapshot date of May 2026, three dynamics defined OppFi's forward trajectory. The first was the litigation pipeline itself: pending state-level true-lender proceedings in multiple jurisdictions represented binary events capable of adding or removing hundreds of millions of dollars of addressable origination volume at a stroke. The second was multi-product expansion — the OppFi Card represented the attempt to capture a longer relationship with borrowers who had moved beyond installment credit, but SalaryTap's pause illustrated how sharply unit economics could punish premature scaling. The third was the broader consumer-credit cycle: any deterioration in employment or a fresh wave of household financial stress would repressurize charge-off rates and constrain origination growth regardless of the legal environment.

The bank-partnership model Todd Schwartz designed in a Chicago office in 2012 had survived fourteen years of regulatory evolution, a punishing credit cycle, and a public-market listing executed at a market peak. Whether the true-lender litigation crucible of 2023–2026 would produce durable legal clarity or continued jurisdictional attrition remained, at the snapshot date, the central unresolved question confronting the platform's second decade.

chapters.title: Litigation, credit cycle, funding, governance, regulatory, competitive risks
chapters.body:
## The True-Lender Crucible

The most existential risk OppFi carried into 2026 was not a credit cycle or an interest-rate shock — it was a question of legal identity. Every loan originated through the bank-partnership model rested on a single contested proposition: that FinWise Bank, Capital Community Bank, or First Electronic Bank, rather than OppFi itself, was the "true lender," and therefore the entity whose home-state preemption rights governed the loan's permissible interest rate. Where that proposition failed in court, OppFi's product — routinely priced between 35% and 160% APR — became instantly unlawful, and the servicer of record became irrelevant.

California opened the most consequential front. After the Department of Financial Protection and Innovation wrote in 2022 that OppFi was operating in the state without the required lender license, OppFi counter-sued in Sacramento Superior Court asserting federal preemption and the "valid-when-made" doctrine — the long-standing common-law principle holding that a loan legal at origination cannot be rendered usurious by subsequent transfer. That doctrine had been codified by the OCC and FDIC in 2020 rules explicitly designed to backstop bank-fintech partnerships, but the Biden administration's CFPB signalled scepticism about their scope, and California courts proved unwilling to treat them as dispositive. Separately, Colorado and Washington state regulators pursued their own true-lender theories, and the District of Columbia's AG brought civil action alleging usurious lending through the bank-partner wrapper. Illinois had already moved earlier: the Predatory Loan Prevention Act of 2021 capped consumer rates at 36% APR, effectively shutting OppFi's core product out of its own home state — a singular irony for a Chicago-headquartered company.

Each adverse outcome compressed OppFi's geographic addressable market in a compounding manner. As [OppFi 10-K filings on SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=OPFI&type=10-K) documented, the company was required to include growing state-by-state disclosure of jurisdictions where it had curtailed or ceased originating loans. By late 2024, the map of inactive or legally contested geographies included several of the most populous US states. Management characterised the situation as a litigation portfolio rather than a regulatory posture — each case individuated, each appealable — but the cumulative effect was that the total-addressable-market number embedded in investor presentations quietly narrowed. The structural asymmetry was punishing: an adverse ruling cost OppFi a state permanently (or until the law changed) while a favourable ruling merely confirmed ground it already held.

## Charge-Off Volatility and the Cycle Scar

The consumer-credit cycle left a deep scar. The 2021 COVID-stimulus vintage was anomalously clean — government transfers suppressed delinquency across the non-prime spectrum — and OppFi, like every platform lender in the space, accelerated originations into that apparent tailwind. The 2022 and early 2023 vintages bore the reversal: inflation eroded the real incomes of borrowers who earned between $30,000 and $60,000 per year, the primary OppFi cohort, and the post-stimulus savings buffer evaporated. Net charge-off rates climbed sharply; provision expenses ballooned; the company swung from profitability to net loss in several quarters before reserve-building peaked and the bad cohorts matured off the portfolio.

Management responded with tighter credit underwriting — raising minimum score thresholds, adjusting state-by-state approval rates, and pulling back on higher-risk segments — a squeeze that constrained origination volume precisely when the stock needed a growth story. The discipline was necessary but its timing was painful: shareholders watched loan balances stagnate and originations compress through mid-2023, and the share price reflected it. The partial recovery in 2024, as cleaner post-tightening cohorts began producing lower provision expense and the charge-off rate normalised toward the low-to-mid twenties range, proved the underwriting pivot had worked, but it also demonstrated how quickly non-prime performance can deteriorate when the macro environment turns. A second consumer-credit dislocation — triggered by rising unemployment or a renewed inflation shock — would restart that cycle.

## Warehouse Risk and Rate Sensitivity

OppFi's funding model amplified both the credit-cycle and rate risks. The company funded its purchase of receivables from bank partners primarily through revolving warehouse credit facilities extended by major bank lenders. Those facilities carried floating-rate pricing, renewing periodically under negotiated terms. The combination of floating-rate cost of funds against a portfolio of fixed-rate consumer loans created structural margin compression whenever short-term rates rose, precisely the condition that prevailed through 2022 and 2023 as the Federal Reserve's tightening cycle pushed SOFR above five percent.

Facility renewal risk compounded the interest-rate exposure. Warehouse lenders reassess counterparty credit quality at renewal, and a platform lender reporting elevated charge-offs and net losses — as OppFi was during the 2022-2023 trough — presents a less attractive borrower than in calmer conditions. The concentration of funding across a limited number of bank facilities meant that a single lender's withdrawal or material tightening of advance-rate terms could force a reduction in origination capacity with little warning. The company disclosed these risks in standard 10-K fashion, but the qualitative language understated the operational reality: warehouse availability was a binding constraint on growth, and its terms moved inversely with OppFi's credit quality.

## Governance: The Up-C Overhang

The corporate structure OppFi adopted in its July 2021 SPAC merger with FG New America introduced governance complexity that persisted as an investor-relations friction point years later. The up-C arrangement placed a holding company — OppFi Inc., the NYSE-listed entity — above an operating LLC whose units were held partly by the public through Class A shares and partly by founder-affiliated entities through Class B shares exchangeable for Class A. Todd Schwartz and related founder parties retained effective voting control through this mechanism, insulating management from activist pressure but also insulating it from market discipline.

The tax receivable agreement embedded in the up-C structure created a separate obligation: as LLC unit holders exchanged their units for Class A shares, the resulting step-up in tax basis generated future tax savings that OppFi Inc. agreed to pay out at an 85% share to the exchanging parties. This obligation, which appeared as a liability on the balance sheet, transferred economic value from public shareholders to insiders at each exchange event. For a company whose shares were already trading at a discount to book value through much of 2022-2024, the TRA overhang reinforced the sense that public minority shareholders occupied a structurally subordinate position.

## Federal Regulatory Exposure and CFPB Dynamics

The federal regulatory landscape shifted meaningfully with the change of administration in January 2025. The CFPB under the Biden administration had been an active antagonist of high-rate bank-partnership lending, pursuing rulemaking on small-dollar credit and publishing interpretive guidance that questioned the scope of federal preemption for fintech-bank arrangements. The Trump administration's move to curtail CFPB enforcement activity in early 2025 reduced the near-term federal regulatory pressure on OppFi's model, but it did not eliminate it — the Bureau's enabling statute remained intact, appropriations litigation notwithstanding, and a future administration could reconstitute its enforcement posture. Congressional Democrats continued to advance versions of the Veterans and Consumers Fair Credit Act, which would impose a 36% APR cap federally across all consumer credit including bank-originated loans, effectively prohibiting OppFi's product nationally. The bill had not passed as of the frozen window, but its periodic reintroduction served as a standing reminder that the regulatory floor beneath the bank-partnership model was political as much as legal.

## Competitive Pressure: Scale, Adjacents, and the Bank-Partnership Squeeze

Enova International entered the frozen window as the largest publicly traded player in the adjacent non-prime online consumer lending space, with materially greater origination volume, a diversified multi-product portfolio spanning consumer and small-business credit, and a balance-sheet lending model that avoided the true-lender exposure inherent in bank partnerships — a structural advantage as the litigation environment worsened. OneMain Financial operated at far larger scale in the near-prime instalment segment and had begun extending modestly down the credit spectrum, creating overlap at the margin.

More subtly, the bank-partnership model itself faced competitive pressure from banks and credit unions that were building proprietary small-dollar instalment products, in some cases using OppFi-like technology providers but retaining the economics. Buy-now-pay-later platforms — Affirm and Klarna at scale, plus a constellation of smaller entrants — were not direct substitutes for a $2,000 instalment loan to a 580-FICO borrower, but they competed for the same consumer's marginal spending dollar and trained that consumer to expect zero-fee point-of-sale credit from better-capitalised counterparties. The BNPL adjacency was more pressure on customer acquisition cost than on direct loan competition, but in a business where marketing expense per funded loan was already one of the largest line items, even modest demand-side substitution at the margin tightened unit economics.

Together, the six risk vectors — state-level litigation, credit-cycle volatility, warehouse funding fragility, governance structure, federal regulatory exposure, and competitive intensity — constituted a risk profile unusual even within the non-prime lending category: a company whose core product legality was actively contested in its largest markets, whose unit economics were acutely sensitive to a consumer borrower base with limited financial resilience, and whose governance gave the founder-CEO near-unilateral authority to navigate all of it.

chapters.title: The next 12 months — catalysts, estimates, and what to watch
chapters.body:
## Twelve months of earnings, litigation verdicts, and rate resets

As OppFi reached the late-May 2026 frozen snapshot, the platform was tracking through what management had characterised as a normalising credit environment — a description encoding both the recovery from the severe 2022-2023 charge-off cycle and the unresolved overhang of state-level true-lender litigation that continues to cap the market's willingness to assign a full earnings multiple to the franchise. The next four quarters will determine whether that normalisation is durable or whether a second deterioration in consumer credit quality, compounded by adverse legal verdicts, forces a reassessment of the platform's addressable market.

## The catalyst calendar: Q2 2026 through Q1 2027

**Q2 2026 earnings (expected early August 2026).** Summer originations are OppFi's highest-volume quarter; the key watch item in the August print will be NCO trajectory on the 2024-2025 cohorts — the vintages underwritten at tighter standards following the 2022-2023 cycle losses. Sustained improvement in the quarterly net charge-off rate toward 40% annualised would signal reserve releases, flow-through operating leverage, and a potential upward revision to the FY2026 EPS range.

**Q3 2026 earnings (expected early November 2026).** The November print is the first window into early delinquency on the summer 2026 vintage. Q3 is historically where consumer credit stress from the peak-origination quarter surfaces in 30- and 60-day buckets. This report will likely include an updated full-year guidance range and the first substantive commentary on 2027 origination capacity.

**Q4 2026 / FY2026 earnings (expected March 2027).** The full-year print is the most consequential filing in the twelve-month window. It establishes whether OppFi's recovery has produced sustainable mid-teens return on equity, and whether OppFi Card receivables have reached a scale that meaningfully diversifies revenue beyond OppLoans installment lending.

**Litigation calendar.** Beyond the earnings schedule, the litigation docket is the highest-variance catalyst in the twelve-month window. As of the frozen snapshot, proceedings challenging the bank-partnership model remained active in Colorado, the District of Columbia, and several additional jurisdictions. A first-instance adverse ruling in a state accounting for material origination volume would likely trigger an immediate suspension and a receivables write-down in that market. An appellate affirmation of OppFi's bank-partnership structure — or a federal preemption ruling — would reduce the discount the market applies to the operating footprint. Either outcome could move the stock more than a full year of quarterly earnings beats or misses combined.

**Regulatory calendar.** The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's stance on bank-partnership models remained contested entering mid-2026. Any formal rulemaking guidance — whether clarifying or restricting the true-lender determination framework — would cascade directly into OppFi's cost of regulatory compliance and its ability to onboard new bank partners. The CFPB's spring and fall regulatory agenda filings are essential monitoring points throughout the period.

## Consensus estimates and implied growth

Wall Street consensus as of the frozen snapshot reflected cautious optimism about the 2026-2027 earnings trajectory, anchored to continued improvement in charge-off rates and moderate origination growth.

| Period | Revenue est. | YoY growth | Adj. EPS est. | YoY growth |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q2 2026E | ~$130M | ~8% | ~$0.18 | ~25% |
| Q3 2026E | ~$128M | ~7% | ~$0.17 | ~21% |
| Q4 2026E | ~$125M | ~6% | ~$0.15 | ~15% |
| Q1 2027E | ~$122M | ~5% | ~$0.14 | ~12% |
| FY2026E | ~$508M | ~7% | ~$0.66 | ~20% |

*Consensus proxies as of the frozen snapshot date; OPFI does not provide quarterly per-share guidance.*

The implied revenue growth — mid-to-high single digits — reflects the market's view that OppFi can grow origination volumes modestly while holding yield compression at bay as consumer credit stabilises. The more aggressive EPS growth rate (approximately 20% for FY2026 versus 7% revenue growth) reflects operating leverage: the servicing platform carries largely fixed technology and compliance costs, so incremental net revenue after provision flows disproportionately to operating income.

The key swing variable is the net revenue margin — total revenue less net charge-offs and warehouse-line interest expense. A 200-basis-point widening in annualised NCO rates from current levels would, by rough calculation, reduce FY2026 net income by 30-40% depending on reserve-release timing, a scenario that would break the consensus EPS range entirely.

## Key metrics to watch each quarter

**Net charge-off rate (annualised NCO%).** The single most important operational variable. OppFi's gross yield on the OppLoans book is compelling — well north of 100% APR blended on the FinWise, Capital Community, and First Electronic origination programs combined — but charge-offs have historically consumed 45-55% of that gross yield in a stressed cycle. Any sequential deterioration in the NCO rate beyond seasonal norms is a leading indicator of earnings risk and should prompt immediate re-evaluation of the reserve-coverage adequacy.

**Auto-approval rate.** The share of applications processed through the automated underwriting engine without manual review is a proxy for credit-model confidence and pricing discipline. A rising auto-approval rate at stable or improving NCO is the signal that the platform is scaling without sacrificing risk management; a rising auto-approval rate accompanied by NCO deterioration is the early warning that growth is being purchased at the expense of vintage quality.

**OppFi Card receivables.** The card product represents OppFi's most credible path to expanding per-customer lifetime value beyond a single installment cycle. Quarterly growth in card receivables and the card-specific NCO rate will determine whether the product builds toward material revenue contribution or remains a de minimis line item. Investors should look for evidence that card users are not simply the highest-risk segment of the OppLoans book migrating to revolving credit.

**Warehouse facility utilisation and spread.** Funding is the operating constraint for a balance-sheet-light origination platform. The utilisation rate and SOFR-spread on warehouse lines is a real-time indicator of both institutional lender confidence in the receivables quality and OppFi's capacity to grow originations without dilutive equity raises.

**State-level origination disclosures.** OppFi reports originations by state in periodic filings. A sudden decline in any state with an active litigation docket should be read as a voluntary suspension pending legal resolution — itself a precursor to a potentially significant addressable-market write-down.

## Beat vs. miss: the quarterly decision tree

A **beat** against current consensus requires: NCO rates at or below 40% annualised on the active book; revenue growth of 10% or more, driven by origination volumes above the base case; OppFi Card receivables growing faster than 15% sequentially; and no new adverse state-level true-lender rulings in the period. Under this scenario, FY2026 adjusted EPS would likely print in the $0.72-0.78 range — 10-18% above consensus — and the stock would re-rate toward 12-14x forward earnings from its currently suppressed litigation-adjusted multiple.

A **miss** requires any combination of: NCO rates drifting above 48% annualised; an adverse ruling in a large state — California residual exposure, New York, or Illinois — that forces an origination suspension; warehouse facility costs rising materially on spread widening; or CFPB rulemaking that formally constrains the bank-partnership origination model. Under this scenario, FY2026 EPS could fall to the $0.45-0.52 range, and multiple compression from the compounding litigation and credit risk would push the stock toward 6-7x forward earnings.

## The asymmetric setup into mid-2027

The bull case rests on the observation that OppFi is fundamentally a technology and risk-management business temporarily discounted by legal uncertainty. If the true-lender framework stabilises — through federal preemption clarity, a string of appellate victories, or simply an extended period without new adverse rulings — the platform's earnings power at current origination volumes supports a materially higher valuation. Management has consistently cited a 60-plus-million-person non-prime consumer market with limited access to conventional credit, a runway that requires no market-share gains from direct competitors such as Enova, OneMain, or Curo to justify meaningful origination growth over a multi-year horizon.

The bear case rests on the structural fragility of the bank-partnership model itself. Every OppFi loan is originated by an FDIC-insured bank partner; every true-lender adverse ruling strips away another state's addressable population. Unlike Enova or OneMain, OppFi cannot pivot to direct lending under a federal charter if the bank-partnership architecture is adjudicated away — it would require a fundamental restructuring of the platform's legal and funding model. In that scenario, the 2026-2027 earnings estimates are not a floor but a ceiling, declining sequentially as each adverse ruling removes another state from the origination map.

At the frozen snapshot, the balance tilted modestly bullish on a twelve-month horizon. The credit cycle recovery was real, the origination technology was proven at scale, and the litigation overhang — while persistent — had not escalated beyond the known-and-priced state docket. The tail risk, however, was genuine. Any portfolio position should be sized with the explicit recognition that a single unfavourable appellate ruling in a large state can compress both earnings and the multiple simultaneously — the double-body-blow scenario that separates a structural value opportunity from a litigation value trap.

chapters.title: Litigation resolution paths, multi-product expansion, 2026-2030 horizon
chapters.body:
## The fork in the road: litigation as the master variable

The strategic horizon for OppFi from 2026 through the end of the decade divided itself into two fundamentally different businesses depending on a single variable: how the accumulated weight of state-level true-lender litigation resolved.

By the mid-2026 frozen window, the company had spent roughly three years contending with coordinated pressure across California, Colorado, Washington D.C., and New York — jurisdictions accounting for a meaningful share of the non-prime consumer population OppFi was built to serve. The legal theory in each venue was substantially the same: that OppFi, not its bank partners — FinWise Bank, Capital Community Bank, or First Electronic Bank — was the "true lender" under state law, and that the loans OppFi serviced therefore had to comply with state usury caps rather than the home-state interest-rate exportation authority granted to federally insured banks under the Depository Institutions Deregulation and Monetary Control Act and the National Bank Act. Each adverse ruling did not merely cost OppFi that state's origination volume; it invited copycat enforcement across the remaining thirty-plus states where the company operated without a legal cloud. Each favourable resolution validated not just OppFi's model but the broader bank-partnership architecture that fintech lenders had constructed across the preceding decade.

## Path A: compression and the adverse-outcome scenario

The pessimistic resolution path required no new legal theory. California's Department of Financial Protection and Innovation had already demonstrated the enforcement template: its 2020 consumer-lending reforms capping most installment loans at 36% effectively rendered OppFi's core product — typically priced between 59% and 160% APR depending on loan characteristics and vintage — unviable if OppFi were deemed the true lender. Colorado adopted similar mechanics through amendments to its Uniform Consumer Credit Code. Under this compression scenario, OppFi's addressable market shrank toward remaining states with no effective usury ceiling, a population concentrated in the South and Midwest.

Management's response, as articulated in SEC filings across the period, centred on three mitigants: deepening penetration in favourable jurisdictions, accelerating fee-based revenue streams that carried lighter credit-rate exposure, and pivoting OppFi's technology platform toward a licensing or white-label configuration that generated servicing income without direct credit exposure. The OppFi Card, crucially, operated under a different regulatory posture — as an FDIC-chartered bank-issued credit card, its rate structure benefited from federal preemption on a more settled legal basis than the installment loan product, giving it survivability the core OppLoans product could not claim with equivalent confidence in an adverse ruling environment.

## Path B: validated model and the expansion scenario

The more optimistic resolution path leaned on what OppFi's legal team and bank partners continued to argue was sound law: that a bank which originates a loan, books it on its own balance sheet, and retains meaningful economic interest is the lender of record irrespective of downstream servicing arrangements. The Valid When Made doctrine, reinforced by OCC and FDIC rulemakings issued in 2020 and 2021 specifically to counteract the uncertainty unleashed by the Second Circuit's *Madden v. Midland Funding* ruling, provided the strongest available federal legal anchor. If the major state cases settled on terms that preserved rate exportation, OppFi's addressable market expanded rather than contracted.

The non-prime consumer population in the United States — roughly 80 million adults carrying FICO scores below 650 — remained chronically underserved by conventional credit. OppFi's origination infrastructure, underwriting models, and servicing platform were purpose-built for this cohort. In the expansion scenario, the litigation years would be recast in retrospect as a forced period of operational discipline that incidentally eliminated undercapitalised bank-partnership competitors who lacked OppFi's legal budget and bank-relationship depth. The company's three-bank origination structure, distributing origination concentration risk across FinWise, Capital Community, and First Electronic, was itself a hedge: if regulators applied pressure to any single bank partner, the program could continue through the remaining two while the challenged relationship was restructured.

## The OppFi Card as hedge and product wedge

Whatever the litigation outcome, the OppFi Card occupied a singular position in the company's portfolio — simultaneously a hedge against adverse true-lender rulings and a product capable of deepening customer relationships beyond the episodic transactional model of installment lending.

OppFi's core business carried a structural limitation: a customer who successfully repaid a $1,500 OppLoans installment loan over twelve months graduated out of the product set precisely as they became a lower-risk, higher-lifetime-value borrower. The Card created a mechanism for retaining that customer — generating recurring interchange revenue while sustaining the data-collection relationship OppFi used to recalibrate its underwriting models continuously. The SalaryTap salary-advance product, paused following challenging unit economics, had represented an earlier attempt to solve the same tenure problem; its suspension underscored that product adjacencies in the non-prime segment demanded careful unit-economics discipline before scale investment.

The Card also carried a more settled regulatory posture. Issued by an FDIC-insured bank partner under the established credit-card framework, its rate structure rested on federal preemption doctrine with a longer and more stable legal history than the installment-loan bank-partnership model. Per-account economics ran lower than a triple-digit APR installment loan, but customer tenure extended, and the recurring rather than episodic revenue stream produced a longer-dated, more predictable cash flow from each acquired account.

## Consumer-credit cycle: the 2026 positioning

By the time OppFi entered its 2026 operating year, the credit cycle that had devastated 2022-2023 vintage cohorts was substantially digested. Charge-off rates — elevated through late 2022 and persistent into 2023 as pandemic-era savings buffers exhausted across the non-prime population — had normalised as new originations were underwritten to tighter standards and as the macro labour market proved more durable than credit-cycle pessimists had forecast.

The 2024 and 2025 vintage books carried lower loss rates, and as those cohorts seasoned, OppFi's income statement absorbed the benefit of improving reserve releases rather than reserve builds. Net revenue per originated dollar improved, and warehouse facilities backing the purchased receivables portfolio — renegotiated at tighter spreads as performance data accumulated — reduced the company's blended cost of capital. The forward question was whether 2026-2027 origination growth could be pursued without re-opening the charge-off cycle; the machine-learning income verification and bank-account connectivity data layered over the traditional FICO signal gave OppFi's models a fuller picture of actual cash-flow position than the static credit file could provide, reducing the precision cost of tighter underwriting.

## The 2026-2030 strategic posture

Across the full 2026-2030 horizon, OppFi's strategic posture as of the frozen window carried a coherent logic regardless of which litigation path prevailed.

In both scenarios, the company was investing in the non-credit-risk dimensions of its business — specifically in technology platform capability, in product breadth beyond OppLoans, and in the proprietary data assets that each repaid-loan cohort deepened in ways competitors without equivalent origination volume could not replicate. The up-C structure, engineered at the July 2021 SPAC combination with FG New America to allow the Schwartz family and original investors to convert their operating-LLC units into Class A NYSE shares over time, created a predictable overhang on public float but left management's operational flexibility intact. The dual-class configuration insulated strategic decision-making from short-cycle shareholder pressure at precisely the moment the litigation environment demanded multi-year resolve.

The competitive field — [Enova International](https://ir.enova.com), Curo Group, OneMain Financial, World Acceptance Corporation — faced analogous pressures, each operating within some version of the bank-partnership or high-rate direct-lending framework and each contending with the same state-by-state regulatory progression. OppFi's differentiation resided less in its loan product itself and more in its thesis that the non-prime consumer deserved a technology-mediated path toward mainstream credit access, not a permanent residence in a high-cost tier. Whether that thesis survived the litigation crucible intact, or was forced into structural adaptation toward a smaller market and a more diversified revenue base, the decade ahead would determine how durable the claim remained — and whether a company that began life in Chicago as Opportunity Financial had, by the time the courts finished with it, built something that justified the name.

## Competitive Set

| Peer | Model | Primary Product |
|------|-------|----------------|
| Enova International | Direct lender + marketplace | Personal loans, SMB lending |
| Curo Group | Direct lender, storefront + online | Payday, installment |
| OneMain Financial | Direct lender | Personal installment loans |
| Elevate Credit | Bank-partnership model | Rise installment, Elastic line of credit |
| World Acceptance Corp. | Direct lender, branch network | Small personal loans |

OppFi's differentiator within this set was its pure-platform posture — marketing, technology, and servicing layered atop FDIC-insured bank partners — which enabled rate exportation under federal preemption but simultaneously concentrated regulatory exposure in the true-lender doctrine.

---

## True-Lender Litigation Status (as of 2026-05-23)

| Jurisdiction | Nature of Challenge | Status |
|--------------|---------------------|--------|
| California | State AG / plaintiff bar: OppFi is the true lender; subject to CA usury caps | Ongoing / contested |
| Colorado | State usury-cap enforcement challenge to bank-partnership model | Ongoing |
| Washington D.C. | District AG action against rent-a-bank arrangements | Ongoing |
| New York | Consumer protection and usury challenges | Ongoing |

Each adverse resolution compresses the addressable non-prime consumer market; each favorable outcome preserves or expands it. This binary litigation pipeline defined OppFi's strategic posture through the 2024–2026 period.

---

## Corporate Structure Reference

OppFi operates as an **Up-C** holding company. Class A shares trade on NYSE as OPFI; Class B shares remain with founder-related entities. Operating-LLC units held by Class B shareholders are exchangeable into Class A shares. Tax distributions to LLC unit holders are a recurring cash obligation under the structure.
